You put something of yours on the stone, and the weather changes: not dramatically, just a wind that had been in your face all morning and now is not.
Going down, you find the way easier than it was coming up, which is not how mountains work, and at the last gate somebody has left {payment} on the post with a stone on top of it so the wind cannot have it.

b.text:
Two hours in the lee of a rock, and then {stranger} comes up the last of the path with a carrier bag and stops dead when they see you.
"You've not moved anything," they say. It is the first thing they check, and they check it properly, on their knees, before they will look at you again.

asides.nurturing: {member} gets them sat down and gets the flask out before any questions get asked.
asides.authoritative: {member} {barks out orders to secure the perimeter|demands status reports on the double|reminds everyone to maintain radio discipline|takes charge of the entry team with a brisk nod}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Ask what it is for.
Offer to carry it up next week.

c.text:
The stones come down easily. Under the bottom one there is a hollow lined with slate, and in the hollow there is a small heavy thing wrapped in oilcloth, and taking it is the easiest theft any of you have ever committed.
The wind gets up while you are doing it. The path down is not where you left it.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

d.text:
The offerings come up from a farm on the south side by a path that is not on any map, and the farm has a wall round it that is far too good for a farm.
The woman there is expecting somebody. She is not especially expecting you, but she has been expecting somebody for a while, and you will do.

choices.text: Take her job.
Ask what happens if nobody takes it.

asides.loyal: {member} {positions themselves between {leader} and the door|nods firmly: "Right behind you, boss."|keeps a watchful eye on {leader}'s blind spot|stands ready to back up whatever call is made}
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b1.text:
"For the col," they say, as if that were the whole answer, and then, because you have waited two hours in the wet: "For what walks it. It has been walked a long time and it does not like being walked on for nothing."
They teach you the four things you leave and the one thing you never leave, and make you say the one thing back.

b2.text:
They look at you for a long moment and then hand you the bag, and it is much heavier than a bag of small objects should be.
You do it for a month. On the fourth week the col leaves something for you, which is not how the arrangement has ever run, and the woman at the farm goes white when she sees it.

d1.text:
The job is to go up in weather she cannot go up in and put a specific thing on a specific stone at a specific hour, and to not look behind you between the col and the second gate.
You do it. You do not look. What is behind you talks the whole way down, pleasantly, about people you have never met, and knows all their names, and one of them is yours.

d2.text:
"Ninety-one," she says. "Ninety-one and then the col comes down here and does the asking itself. It did it in {timeAgo} and there is nothing left of the house it asked at but the gate."
She pays you to make the week's climb once, which is all you are willing to promise, and pays over the odds for it.

a_m.text:
Leaving something of your own on the stone takes {four seconds|a moment|no deciding}, and the wind that had been in your face all morning goes round behind you.
The thing you left is not where you left it. It has been moved {three stones down|to the base ring|into the ring with the heavy ones}, which is where the heavy things go, and it is not heavy.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{It has been sorted. By something. Just now.|It graded our offering.|Whatever grades that cairn is standing here.}"
asides.any: {member} {puts a second thing on the top stone to see|watches the ring rather than the top|steps back off the col}

choices.text: Take the hint. Walk on.
Work out what the sorting is by.
Put it back on the top stone.

a_sort.text:
It is not by weight and it is not by value. It is by {how much it cost the person who left it|what it was worth to give|how much was given up}, which is a thing the cairn can apparently measure and nobody else can.
Which means the base ring is the expensive ring, and the base ring is {full|packed|four deep}, and the people of this valley have been paying a great deal more up here than anybody down there admits.

a_back.text:
It goes back on the top stone and stays there for {nine seconds|a count of nine|about as long as it takes to step back}.
Then the wind comes round into your face again, harder, and the whole col does the thing a room does when you have been rude in it, and the walk down is {two hours|an hour|the longest} of everybody being very careful about their footing.

c_m.text:
The stones come down easily. Under the bottom one there is a hollow lined with slate, and in the hollow there is a small heavy thing wrapped in oilcloth.
There is also {a second hollow|room for another|an empty slate box}, beside it, the same size, lined the same way, and it has clearly held something and does not now.

choices.text: Take it and rebuild the cairn badly.
Take it and rebuild the cairn properly, stone for stone.
Find out what came out of the second hollow.

c_build.text:
Rebuilding a cairn properly means putting every stone back on its own bed, in its own order, which takes {four hours|the rest of the light|until dusk} and is done by people who are not masons and get it right anyway.
Nobody in the valley ever knows it was opened. The thing in the oilcloth is worth what it is worth, and the party is the only party ever to have taken something off that col and left it exactly as they found it.

c_second.text:
The wear in the second hollow says it held its thing for a very long time and lost it {recently|inside the year|this season}, and the slate is scratched on the way out rather than the way in.
Somebody took it. Somebody who knew the cairn was a lid. That is a much more interesting fact than the object in the party's hand, and it is one that can be followed.

e_mountainice.title: {The Crevasse|Forty Metres Down And Still Talking|The Rope Somebody Left}

n0.text:
A rope, anchored properly, ice screws in sound ice, going down into a crevasse and pulled tight.
Someone's on the other end of it. Somebody has been on the other end of it for a while, judging by the ice that has formed on the rope where it crosses the lip.
When you get to the edge and look, a voice comes up from a long way down, conversational, unhurried, and says: "Is that you, then?"
The screws are in sound ice and they are {new|this season's|not twenty years old}, and the rope is old.
n0.emText:
A rope going down into a crevasse, tight, iced over at the lip. Down there, a voice, unhurried: "Is that you, then?"
You have never heard the voice. It knows you. That is now the fourth thing this month that has known you when you did not know it, and you are keeping count, because counting is the only archive you have.
n0.bubba: Bubba lies flat and shouts down the hole. "WHO'S ASKIN'?" A pause. "He says he knows ya, sugar. Uh-uh. Nun me piace."

asides.brave: {member} {steps up front with a weapon ready: "I'll take point."|grins and racks the slide: "Let's see what wants to die today."|is already at the hatch before anyone can argue|steps over the threshold without flinching}
asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Go down.
Talk to it from the top.
Haul the rope up and see what is on the end.
Cut the rope.

a.text:
Forty metres down the blue goes very dark and then opens: a chamber in the ice with a shelf of gear on it, twenty years of it, arranged.
The man on the end of the rope is sitting on the shelf. He is not cold. He offers you the thermos. He has been down here since a date he gives cheerfully and which is on the wrong side of what a person survives.

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.nurturing: {member} tries to get a coat on him. He does not need it. {member} does it anyway.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Take him up.
Take the gear and leave him where he is comfortable.
Ask him what he is waiting for.

b.text:
He talks for forty minutes and he is very good company.
He knows the names of two of your party, one of them a name they have not used since they were a child. He is not showing off. He is filling a silence, the way people do who have been alone a while, and every so often he stops mid-word and waits for a sound that does not come.

choices.text: Ask what he is listening for.
Promise to send help and go.

asides.melancholic: {member} sits at the lip long after the rest of you have got cold.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
It comes up light, and it keeps coming, and it keeps coming: a hundred and ten metres of rope out of a crevasse that is sixty deep, and on the end of it a harness, buckled, with nobody in it and no wear on the leg loops.
The voice, still down there, says: "Ah. Well."

d.text:
You cut it, and the end goes down without a sound, and the voice does not shout.
It says, quite kindly, "That's all right," and then nothing at all, and the crevasse is a hole in a glacier on a cold afternoon.
One of your party does not sleep properly for a fortnight and will not say which part of it is the problem.

a1.text:
He comes up easily. He weighs about as much as a coat.
At the lip, in daylight, he thanks each of you by name, walks eleven paces onto the snow, and is not there. The gear you brought up with him is entirely real and worth a fortune to the right museum.

a2.text:
Forty years of mountaineering hardware, all of it good, some of it made by firms that closed before you were born.
He helps you pack it and holds the rope while you go up, which is the part that stays with you.

a3.text:
"The rest of the rope," he says.
Then he explains, patiently, what he means, and it takes some time, and by the end of it you are quite certain that the ice has been keeping him not out of kindness but out of an agreement, and that you have been handed the terms.

b1.text:
"The second one," he says. "There's always a second one on a rope. I keep listening for the second one."
Zero second anchor. There never was. What comes up the rope when you finally stop talking is not him.

b2.text:
You promise, and you mean it, and the rescue service in {region} takes the grid reference and looks at each other in a way you will think about later.
They have that reference. They have had it for a long time. They pay your expenses, take a statement, and ask you, very carefully, whether he used your names.

a2_m.text:
Forty years of mountaineering hardware, all of it good, some of it made by firms that closed before you were born, and he helps you pack it and holds the bag open.
While he holds it he asks, without any weight on the question at all, whether the party would mind leaving {one thing|a single item|something of theirs} on the shelf, because the shelf {has to have something on it|cannot be empty|is not allowed to be empty}.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Do not put anything of ours on that shelf.|He is very relaxed about forty years of his own kit.|That shelf is the point. Not the gear.}"
asides.any: {member} {looks at the shelf and then at the man|keeps packing|holds one thing back without being asked}

choices.text: Leave something. It is a fair trade.
Take the gear and leave nothing.
Ask what happens to a shelf that is empty.

a2_leave.text:
One item off the party's own kit, put on the shelf in the gap the bag came out of, and he straightens it {slightly|by a finger's width|so it sits square}.
The climb out is easy in a way the climb in was not. The item is on the shelf for good and everybody knows it. Whichever of the party put it there dreams about a blue room {four|five|several} times a year for the rest of their life and does not mind.

a2_empty.text:
"Then it is a hole in the ice," he says, reasonably, "and holes in ice want filling, and there is nothing down here to fill it with except what walks in."
He is not threatening anybody. He is explaining a system he has been maintaining, alone, for {forty years|four decades|longer than that}, and he would very much like to be relieved, and he says so, out loud, for the first time.

b2_m.text:
The promise is made and it is meant, and the walk down takes {four hours|the rest of the day|until dark}, and the rescue service in {region} takes the grid reference.
They look at each other. Then one of them opens a folder that is {two inches|very} thick, and turns it round on the desk, and the grid reference at the top of the first page is the one the party has just given them.

choices.text: Take the money for the report and leave it with them.
Read the folder.
Go back up with them.

b2_folder.text:
{Nine|Eleven|A great many} call-outs to the same grid reference over {thirty years|three decades|a long time}, every one of them a rope going down into a crevasse with a voice on the end of it, every one of them closed as a recovery with nothing recovered.
And the names of the teams. Two of the names are on the current duty board in the next room, and neither of them will talk about it, and one of them goes outside.

b2_back.text:
Going back up with the service means going up with {four|five} people who have done this before and who do not talk on the way.
They bring up a rope. There is nothing on the end of it. They coil it, log it, and go back down, and on the way one of them says, to nobody, that the second anchor is the part everybody gets wrong, and the party does not ask what that means until much later.

e_mountaindesert.title: {The Stair|Two Hundred Steps Cut Into Nothing|The Ladder In The Rock}

n0.text:
Steps cut into the rock face, going up: two hundred of them, worn in the middle, ending at a ledge with nothing on it and nowhere to go.
No temple. No door. No niche. A ledge, an arm's length deep, two hundred steps above the valley floor, and worn steps mean feet, and a lot of them.
At the bottom, in the shade, somebody has left a water jar. It is full.
The two hundredth step is worn like the others. Nothing has ever stood on it long enough to wear it and gone no further.
n0.emText:
Two hundred steps cut into a cliff, worn hollow in the middle, and at the top a ledge with nothing on it at all.
Something used to be there. You are becoming an expert on the shape of things that used to be there. At the bottom of the stair, in the shade, a full water jar, put down today by somebody who expects the walk to be made.
n0.bubba: Bubba drinks from the jar, which everyone would have advised against. "Ah. Fresh. Somebody's mindin' this place. Statte accuorto ncoppa, sugar."

asides.disciplined: {member} {follows standard breach protocol by the book|clears every corner with military precision|keeps a steady firing stance and monitors the sensors|checks the ammo count and maintains position}
asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.hedonistic: {member} wants to know why anybody would climb two hundred steps for a ledge.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Climb and stand on the ledge.
Wait at the bottom for whoever fills the jar.
Search the foot of the cliff for what fell off the ledge.
Climb at night.

a.text:
The valley from up here is the whole of the world laid flat, and the ledge is exactly deep enough to stand on with your back to the rock, which is what it is for.
When you have been there long enough for your breathing to settle, the rock behind your shoulders is warm, and there is a hollow in it at the height of a head, worn by heads.

choices.text: Put your head in the hollow.
Come down and say nothing about it.

asides.calm: {member} has already got their head in the hollow and their eyes shut.
asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
The jar is filled by a boy of about eleven who runs the last hundred metres because he is late, and who is not remotely bothered by finding four strangers there.
"It's my week," he says. "You have to keep it full. If it's empty they come down."
He says this the way you would say that the bins go out on Tuesday.

choices.text: Ask who they are.
Empty the jar and wait.
Fill it, and fill the spare, and go.

asides.nurturing: {member} carries the water the last hundred metres for him, obviously.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text: Two hundred steps of dropped things: coins from six centuries, buttons, a shoe, four rings, a knife with a saint's name on the blade, and, half under a slab, in {relicWord}, something that was not dropped but hidden.

d.text:
At night the steps are cold and the ledge is not.
Standing on it in the dark, you can see the valley the way it was: lights in a pattern of a town that is not there, and a road going somewhere that has not existed in four hundred years, and, on the ledge with you, the shoulder-to-shoulder press of a queue.
Nobody pushes. You are, however, in the way.

a1.text: Leaning against the warm rock, you get a sudden sharp clarity: four minutes of knowing exactly where you are, in a sense of the word 'where' that includes the year, and coming out of it you can feel the size of the mistake you have been making about something.

a2.text:
You come down without mentioning it and somebody at the bottom takes one look at your face and hands you the water jar without a word.
Whatever the ledge does, it does not do it to everybody, and the people who keep the jar full have known that for four hundred years.

b1.text:
"The ones on the stair," he says, and then will not be drawn further, except to say that his grandmother saw them and that they {Walk in|Step through the entrance|Cross the threshold|Head inside} a queue and that you must never be on the steps when they are, because there is only one width of stair.
He tells you when, which is the useful part, and it is tonight.

b2.text:
You tip it out on the stones and the boy goes white and runs, which is the correct response, and which you will remember.
They come down. There is only one width of stair, and you are on it.

b3.text:
You fill both jars and carry them up to the second landing where they are supposed to sit, and the boy talks the whole way about a bicycle he is saving for.
At the bottom his mother is waiting with the whole family, who knew you were coming before you did, and who feed you until you cannot stand.

c_m.text:
Two hundred steps of dropped things, worked over on hands and knees in the shade: coins from six centuries, buttons, a shoe, four rings, a knife with a saint's name on the blade.
And, half under the bottom step, a jar. Not the water jar: an older one, the same shape, broken, and {full of|packed with|holding} the same small objects that are on the cairn-stone of every col in this country.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Same offerings, different mountain.|Somebody has been running this system for a while.|Six centuries of people paying the same toll.}"
asides.any: {member} {lays the coins out by century|turns the broken jar over|counts the rings}

choices.text: Bag the lot and go.
Date the contents of the broken jar.
Take nothing. Put the good jar back where the broken one was.

c_date.text:
Six centuries is wrong. The oldest thing in the jar is {two thousand years|considerably older|older than the language the saint's name is in}, and the newest is {this year|from this spring|recent}, and there is no gap anywhere in the sequence.
Nothing in this country has been continuous for two thousand years. This has. That is the finding, and it is worth more than every coin in the party's hands.

c_jar.text:
The whole jar, filled at the spring, carried up and set into the hollow under the bottom step where the broken one has sat for {however long|a very long time|nobody knows how long}.
The party takes not one coin off that cliff. On the way down through the village a woman none of them have spoken to puts bread and cheese into {leader}'s hands and closes the door before anyone can say anything.

b3_m.text:
Both jars filled, and carried up to the second landing where they are supposed to sit, with the boy talking the whole way about a bicycle he is saving for.
At the second landing there are {four|five} jars already, all of them full, all of them fresh, and the boy says the others are not his, and that he does not know whose they are, and that they are always there.

choices.text: Set the jars down and go back down with him.
Wait at the landing to see who brings the others.
Carry a jar to the top. All two hundred steps.

b3_wait.text:
Four hours on a landing halfway up a cliff in the heat, with the boy gone home and the jars sitting there getting warm.
Nobody comes. At {dusk|the hour the light goes|about seven} there are {six|seven} jars on the landing, and the party has been looking at the landing the entire time, and nobody has come.

b3_top.text:
Two hundred steps with a full jar and no free hand is a different climb from two hundred steps with two free hands, and the last {forty|thirty} are done very slowly.
The jar goes on the ledge. There is nowhere on the ledge for it to go and it goes somewhere anyway, and the hollow in the rock at head height is {warm|warmer|hot} and the valley below is briefly and entirely silent.

e_desert.title: {The Buried Convoy|Eleven Lorries And No Cargo|The Sand Has Moved Again}

n0.text:
The sand has moved and given something back: cab roofs, in a line, eleven of them, a convoy nose to tail under the dune with the drivers' doors all standing open.
The paint is Collective. The plates are four different countries. The tyres are perfect.
The heat is still coming up out of the ground and the metal is cold.
Eleven cabs, and the doors are open on the {left|driver's} side of each of them, and the sand inside the cabs is level with the sand outside.
n0.emText:
Eleven lorry cabs in a line under a moved dune, doors open, tyres perfect, metal cold in a desert.
The whole convoy is holding its breath and has been for years. You know that state. It is the state you woke up in: everything preserved, nothing explained, and the doors open as though whoever left did it in a hurry that has since become permanent.
n0.bubba: Bubba climbs into the first cab like a man buying a truck. "Diesel's still in her. Keys in it. Aoh. Chesta e' 'na trappola, sugar, but she'd start."

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.cautious: {member} {watches the perimeter with a frown: "Bad idea."|checks their weapon charge and backs up a step|keeps a finger on the safety and mutters a warning|eyes the surroundings: "This has trap written all over it."}
asides.grumpy: {member} {complains loudly about the freezing temperature|curses under their breath at the terrible footing|mutters that this job isn't worth the hazard pay|kicks a piece of debris and grunts in frustration}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Dig out a trailer and see what the cargo was.
Start one of them.
Strip the convoy for parts and fuel.
Follow the footprints out.

a.text:
Two hours of digging in the shade of a dune and the trailer doors come clear.
Inside: crates, stencilled with a franchise mark somebody has scratched off, and every crate is empty, and every crate was opened from the inside.

asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Open the rest.
Take the crate marks to somebody who knows the franchise.

b.text:
It turns over on the fourth try and catches, and the noise of a diesel engine in that silence is obscene.
Every other cab in the line starts. All ten of them, one after another, down the row, in order, and then they idle, and the ten empty cabs sit there running.
b.bubba: "Nope," says Bubba, already reversing out of the door. "Nope nope nope. Jamme. Jamme ja'."

asides.brave: {member} {steps up front with a weapon ready: "I'll take point."|grins and racks the slide: "Let's see what wants to die today."|is already at the hatch before anyone can argue|steps over the threshold without flinching}
asides.timid: {member} is back at the dune crest before the fourth one has caught.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Drive yours out.
Turn them all off, one by one, in order.

c.text:
Fuel, filters, batteries, eleven sets of tools, four spare wheels and enough copper to matter.
It takes all afternoon and you are careful and you leave the cabs otherwise as you found them, and a man in {region} buys the lot without asking a single question, which he charges you for by paying less.

d.text:
Eleven sets of prints leave the convoy and go out into the sand together, and stay together, and do not scatter, and at about a kilometre they stop.
Not fade. Stop, all eleven, mid-stride, in a line abreast, facing the same way, which is the way you came.

choices.text: Stand where they stopped and face the way they faced.
Dig where they stopped.

asides.fatalistic: {member} {sighs: "Well, we were going to die eventually."|shrugs: "If the reactor blows, at least it's quick."|mutters that the universe always finds a way to ruin your day|expects the worst and isn't disappointed}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

a1.text: Every trailer, the same: opened from inside, and in the ninth one, still in there, the thing that did the opening, which has been out here a long time on nothing at all and which is extremely interested in the arrival of something with blood in it.

a2.text:
The franchise mark belongs to a Collective operation that stopped filing returns in {timeAgo}.
A loss adjuster in {region} has been carrying this convoy on his books for years and pays you handsomely for the coordinates, the photographs and the exact wording of the stencil.

b1.text:
You drive out with ten engines idling behind you and they are still idling when the dune closes the mirror.
It is a good lorry. It is worth real money. For a year afterwards it will not start for anybody but whoever turned that key.

b2.text:
Down the line, one at a time, in order, and each one dies as you reach it and the next one is already quieter, as though it were being asked politely rather than switched off.
The last cab does not have a key in it. It has a hand on the wheel. It thanks you.

d1.text:
You stand in the line abreast with the eleven and face the convoy, and for about ninety seconds the desert is not a desert but a road at night with headlights coming, and every one of you sees it.
What happened to eleven drivers happened over about four seconds. You get the four seconds. You also get what they dropped when it happened.

d2.text:
A metre down: sand, then a floor. Tiled. Warm.
A metre further along, a hatch, and the hatch has been opened from underneath eleven times by eleven pairs of hands, and never opened from the top by anybody.

b1_m.text:
Yours goes into gear and pulls out of the line and the other ten sit there idling, and the mirror fills with {eleven|ten} sets of lights that nobody switched on.
At about {four hundred metres|a quarter of a mile|the first rise} the ten of them move off together, in convoy, nose to tail, {behind you|in the mirror|at the same speed}, keeping station.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{They are not following. They are in convoy.|We are the lead lorry now.|Whatever this run was, we have joined it.}"
asides.any: {member} {watches the mirror and stops narrating|checks the fuel|winds the window down to listen}

choices.text: Keep driving. Keep the lead.
Pull over and let them pass.
Read the run. Where was this convoy going?

b1_pass.text:
Pulling over in open desert and watching ten lorries go past at {forty|thirty|a steady} is a thing that takes {nine minutes|a quarter of an hour|a long time} and is not survivable as a memory.
The last one stops level with the cab. The door on the driver's side opens. Nothing gets out, and nothing gets in, and after a while it closes and the convoy goes on over the rise and the lights go out one by one.

b1_run.text:
The tacho in the lead cab is still legible and the route card is in the door pocket and the run is {four hundred kilometres|a long haul|two days} to a depot that is on the map and is still there.
Driving it, the whole run, with ten lorries behind, takes {two days|a day and a half|thirty hours}, and the depot gate is opened at dawn by a man who counts eleven and then sits down on the step.

d1_m.text:
Standing in the line abreast with the eleven and facing the convoy, the desert is not a desert for about ninety seconds but a road at night with lights on it.
When it stops being that, there are {eleven|ten|a line of} depressions in the sand around the party's boots, and they are the shape of people kneeling, and they are fresh.

choices.text: Walk back to the convoy without looking down again.
Kneel.
Read the ground properly before moving.

d1_kneel.text:
Four people kneel in a desert facing a buried convoy because the sand suggested it, which is either the stupidest or the most correct thing anybody does this year.
The ninety seconds come back and this time they last {eleven minutes|a quarter of an hour|a great deal longer}, and there is a road, and there are eleven drivers on it, and one of them turns round.

d1_read.text:
The depressions are not fresh. They are {old|very old|from the day} and they have been under the sand and the sand has just come off them, which is not how sand works and is exactly how this dune has been behaving all week.
Underneath the kneeling marks, a hand's depth down, the sand stops and the {floor|tile|something flat} starts, and it is the same floor that is a metre down where the prints stop.

e_badlands.title: {The Bone Bed|Everything Here Died Facing The Same Way|The Wash Below The Rim}

n0.text:
A flash flood has cut a new channel and opened a bone bed in the side of it: hundreds of animals, layered, and every skull turned the same way.
Half of them are species that should not be in the same century as each other. All of them are facing the rim of the canyon, where there is a gap in the rock like a doorway with nothing behind it.
{smell}, and under your boots the ground is warm.
Every skull is turned the same way and the way they are turned is {up the wash|at the rim|towards the gap}.
n0.emText:
A new channel cut by a flood, and in its wall a bone bed: hundreds of animals from centuries that should not touch, all of them facing the same gap in the rim.
They were all looking at the same thing when it happened to them. You have never been able to find out what you were looking at.
n0.bubba: Bubba crouches at the layer line with his hat pushed back. "That's a whole lotta critters agreein' on somethin'. Uh-huh. E nun era 'na bella cosa."

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
asides.artistic: {member} says it is a congregation. It is exactly the right word and nobody thanks them for it.
asides.fatalistic: {member} {sighs: "Well, we were going to die eventually."|shrugs: "If the reactor blows, at least it's quick."|mutters that the universe always finds a way to ruin your day|expects the worst and isn't disappointed}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Go up to the gap in the rim.
Dig the bed out properly and see what is in the layers.
Take a skull and go. Museums pay.
Camp here and see what happens after dark.

a.text:
It takes an hour to get up, and from the top the gap is not a gap: it is a doorway, worked, with a lintel, and the rock either side has been shaped and then weathered for as long as the bones have been down there.
Through it, the badlands. The same badlands. Slightly the wrong colour.

asides.cautious: {member} {watches the perimeter with a frown: "Bad idea."|checks their weapon charge and backs up a step|keeps a finger on the safety and mutters a warning|eyes the surroundings: "This has trap written all over it."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Step through.
Block it. Bring the lintel down.

b.text:
Three days of work in two hours, because the flood has done most of it.
Layer four has a horse in it wearing tack. Layer seven has a man, curled, with his arms over his head, holding a tin box. Layer nine is not animals at all.

choices.text: Open the tin box.
Dig down to layer nine.

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
You take one clean skull out of layer two, wrap it properly and carry it out.
The museum in {region} is delighted, pays well, and asks for the location, which you give. Four months later there is no bone bed: there is a fence, a Foundation seal, and a man on a folding chair who has been told your name.

d.text:
After dark the warm ground gets warmer and the bones in the wall do not move, which is important, because everything else does: your shadows, thrown by the fire, go the wrong way and lie flat against the bone bed and stay there when you stand up.
At some point in the small hours the whole herd, all of it, all the layers at once, turns to face the rim again, with a sound like a book being shut.

a1.text:
The same country, the same hour, and no bone bed in the wash: the wall is clean rock, uncut, unflooded.
You are through for about ninety seconds before the doorway behind you starts to close, and you get back with everybody, and one of you is carrying something that was picked up on the other side and which does not exist on this one.

a2.text:
It takes both the crowbar and everything anybody has that goes bang.
The lintel comes down and the doorway is a heap of rock, and down in the wash every skull in the wall turns, all together, to face where it used to be, which is the worst applause any of you will ever receive.

b1.text:
A tin box held by a man who had time to curl up: inside it, dry, {paper}, and a ring, and a photograph of a doorway in a canyon rim with eleven people standing under it.
One of them is holding the tin box. The photograph is older than photography.

b2.text:
Layer nine is worked stone, laid, with a floor and a drain and a doorway of its own, and the animals above it are not a bone bed at all.
They are a roof.

c_m.text:
One clean skull out of layer two, wrapped properly and carried out, which takes {an hour|no time|about an hour} and is the easiest money in the badlands.
The museum in {region} is delighted and pays well, and then the curator turns it over under the lamp and goes quiet, because there is a mark cut into the bone {behind the jaw|under the crest|at the base} and it is a mason's mark.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Somebody signed a horse.|That is a maker's mark on a dead animal.|Whoever laid that bed laid it.}"
asides.any: {member} {asks to see it under the lamp|photographs the mark|says nothing and looks at the curator}

choices.text: Take the money and let them keep it.
Match the mark against the region's masons.
Buy it back and take it to the bone bed.

c_mark.text:
It is on {four|five} churches in this country and on a bridge, and all of them are the work of one family, and the family is still in the trade and still uses the mark.
The current holder of it looks at the photograph for {nine seconds|a long moment|a while}, asks where it was found, and then asks the party to sit down, which is the beginning of something that runs for years.

c_back.text:
Buying it back costs more than it sold for, because museums are museums, and carrying it {two days|a long way|back out} to the wash costs the rest of the week.
It goes back in layer two, in its own socket, turned the way the others are turned. The bed is {four metres|a good deal} more exposed than it was and nothing further has come out of it in any year since.

b2_m.text:
Layer nine is worked stone, laid, with a floor and a drain and a doorway of its own, and the animals above it are not a bone bed at all: they are {fill|packing|what was put on top}.
The drain is clear. It has been kept clear, which is not something a buried floor does for itself, and there is {no silt|nothing|not a handful of dirt} in a channel that has been under a flood plain for {eleven thousand|a great many} years.

choices.text: Take what is on the floor and get out of the hole.
Follow the drain.
Work out what the fill was meant to do.

b2_drain.text:
The drain is {a metre|not quite a metre|low} and runs {sixty metres|a long way|further than anybody is comfortable with} on hands and knees in water that is moving the wrong way, which is to say uphill.
It comes out in a chamber with a floor that is dry and swept, and the party is standing in the middle of it before anybody works out that the water is being pumped.

b2_fill.text:
The fill is graded: big animals at the bottom, small at the top, in layers of {four|five}, and it is not a burial and it is not a flood.
It is insulation. Somebody put a metre and a half of dead animals over a floor to keep the temperature in the room below it steady, and they were careful about it, and it has worked for eleven thousand years.

e_tundra.title: {The Survey Stake|Somebody Marked This Out For Something|Grid Reference In The Moss}

n0.text:
Survey stakes in the moss, orange tops, in a grid: a hundred metres by four hundred, marked out for a building nobody is ever going to build out here.
They are new. The moss has not closed round them. There is a portable toilet at the corner of the grid and a wheelbarrow with a wheel missing, and no other sign of any human being for sixty kilometres.
{sound}, a long way off, and it does not stop when you stop.
The project number on the stakes is the same number on {four|five} other grids in this country, and none of them have ever been built on either.
n0.emText:
A survey grid staked out in the moss, a hundred by four hundred, brand new, sixty kilometres from anybody. A portable toilet at the corner. A broken wheelbarrow.
Someone's going to build something here and they have not told the ground. The moss knows. You can feel the shape of the argument, the way you can feel a room where two people have just stopped shouting.
n0.bubba: Bubba tips the portaloo door open with a boot, looks in, and shuts it fast. "Nah. Occupied. Uh-uh. Non ce trasite."

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.grumpy: {member} {complains loudly about the freezing temperature|curses under their breath at the terrible footing|mutters that this job isn't worth the hazard pay|kicks a piece of debris and grunts in frustration}
asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Open the portable toilet.
Walk the grid and find the centre.
Pull every stake and stack them.
Follow the sound.

a.text:
It is clean, and it is stocked, and there is a chair in it instead of the usual, and on the chair there is a coat, and in the coat there is a wallet, four keys and a photograph of the grid you are standing in with somebody's arm round somebody in the middle of it.
The photograph is dated four months from now.

choices.text: Take the wallet and the photograph.
Sit in the chair.

asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
The centre of the grid is a patch where the moss is dead in a circle four metres across, and in the middle of it, driven flush with the ground, one stake with no orange top.
Around it, at the eight compass points, eight small piles of stones, made by hand, recently, by somebody who knows this is not how you mark a survey.

choices.text: Pull the flush stake.
Add a ninth pile and wait.

asides.fatalistic: {member} {sighs: "Well, we were going to die eventually."|shrugs: "If the reactor blows, at least it's quick."|mutters that the universe always finds a way to ruin your day|expects the worst and isn't disappointed}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
A hundred and sixty stakes, stacked, in an hour and a half.
The moss closes over the holes within minutes: you can watch it doing it. And when the last stake is out, the sound you have been hearing all afternoon stops, and something eight kilometres off starts walking towards you across ground that takes two days to cross.

d.text:
Ninety minutes' walk. It is a generator, running, chained to a sledge, with no fuel line and no fuel, and it is warm, and it has been running like this since somebody left it.
It is powering a single cable that goes into the ground and does not come out.

choices.text: Dig the cable up.
Stop the generator.

a1.text:
You are eleven kilometres away when somebody uses the name on the wallet to call across the tundra, once, clearly, in a voice that carries the way voices do not.
The wallet has three hundred in it and a card that is worth more than three hundred to the right office. The photograph you keep. In four months you will look at it again.

a2.text:
You sit down in a portable toilet in the middle of the tundra with the door open, because you are the kind of person who follows a thing through.
What you get, over about four minutes, is the whole project: what is going to be built here, who is paying, what is under the grid that they want to be on top of, and why they brought a chair.

b1.text:
It comes up two metres long, sharpened, iron, and old: older than the survey, older than the project number, older than the orange paint by centuries.
It was here first. The survey grid is centred on it because whoever laid the grid found it and built the whole job round it, and the eight piles are somebody's attempt to keep it in the ground.

b2.text:
You build a ninth pile at the centre, over the flush stake, and sit down, and nothing happens for two hours.
Then the moss closes over your pile, and over all eight, and the dead circle greens in front of you at the speed of a tide coming in, and the survey stakes at the edge of the grid fall over, all of them, in one long clatter going round.

d1.text:
It goes down four metres and ends in a plate, and the plate is bolted to something that is not a rock.
What you get out of it before the generator stops on its own is a coil of cable, a plate of an alloy that does not belong to this decade, and a very strong sense of having interrupted something halfway.

d2.text:
You kill it, and the silence is enormous, and every stake in the grid ninety minutes behind you goes over at once. You hear it. Across ninety minutes of tundra, you hear it.
When you get back the moss has closed and the portable toilet is gone and the wheelbarrow has both its wheels.

a1_m.text:
The wallet goes in the pack, and the photograph with it, and the party is {four kilometres|a couple of miles|well} out before anybody looks at the photograph properly.
It is of this grid. The stakes are in it, and the moss is in it, and so is the portable toilet, and so are {four|five} people standing where the party was standing, and it is {forty years old|old|much older than the stakes}.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Same grid. Same stakes. Forty years.|Somebody has done this before us.|Put it back. Put it all back.}"
asides.any: {member} {turns the photograph over looking for a date|counts the people in it|looks back the way they came}

choices.text: Keep it all. Keep walking.
Read the back of the photograph.
Take it back to the coat.

a1_back.text:
There is writing on the back in pencil and it is {four names|five names|a list of names}, and the last one on the list is the name in the wallet, and it has been written in a different hand and more recently than the others.
Which means the list is kept, and it is kept by whoever comes after, and the party is holding a pencil and standing in a survey grid in the middle of the tundra with the moss closing over their own boot prints.

a1_return.text:
Eleven kilometres back, and the coat is on the chair, and the wallet goes into the coat and the photograph goes back into the wallet, and the door is shut properly.
Nobody calls across the tundra that night. Nobody calls the next night either. The party sleeps badly for {a fortnight|some weeks|a while} out of sheer anticipation and nothing ever comes of it, which is the best available outcome and is very hard to enjoy.

d2_m.text:
Killing the generator takes {four seconds|one movement|a hand on the switch} and the silence afterwards is enormous.
Then, ninety minutes behind, every stake in the grid goes over at once, and it is audible across that distance, which is not a thing that noise does out here.

choices.text: Keep walking. It is done.
Start the generator again.
Go back to the grid at a run.

d2_start.text:
It starts on the first pull, with no fuel line and no fuel, as though it had been waiting to be asked.
Ninety minutes away the stakes stand back up. The party hears that too. Nobody in the party ever tells this part of the story at a fire, and the generator is still running out there as far as anybody knows.

d2_run.text:
Ninety minutes at a run over moss is {two hours|longer than ninety minutes|a bad two hours}, and the grid, when it comes up, is flat: a hundred and sixty stakes lying down, all pointing the same way, at the centre.
The dead circle at the centre is {twice the size|four metres wider|bigger}, and the flush stake is standing proud of the ground by a hand's width, and it is coming up on its own.

e_permafrost.title: {The Thaw|What The Ground Is Giving Back|Fourteen Metres Of Held Breath}

n0.text:
The ground is going soft for the first time in eleven thousand years and it is giving things back.
A post, upright, worked with a blade. A boat, or the ribs of one, a hundred kilometres from water. And a hand: a human hand, brown, perfect, at the end of an arm that is still in the ice, and the fingers are closed on something.
The smell is not decay. It is more like {smell}.
The thaw is a strip, not a patch, and a strip means something is {running under it|warm underneath|being followed}.
n0.emText:
Eleven thousand years of held ground going soft, and everything it has been holding coming up at once: a carved post, the ribs of a boat, and a hand out of the ice with its fingers shut on something.
The ground here has better memory than you do and it is losing it in a single season, and you can feel exactly how that feels from the inside.
n0.bubba: Bubba takes his hat off to the hand, seriously, no joke in it. "Signo'. Requiem. Awright. Now let's see what he's holdin'."

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.melancholic: "He was carrying it," {member} says. "Whatever it is, he was carrying it when it got him."
asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Open the hand.
Dig the arm out. Get all of him.
Follow the strip of thaw.
Take the post. It is the only thing you can carry.

a.text:
The fingers give like cold wax, one at a time, and what is in the palm is a bead of something dark that is warm, and that gets warmer the longer it is out of the ice.
Behind you, the thaw accelerates. You can hear it: water moving under a metre of ground for a hundred metres in every direction.

choices.text: Keep the bead.
Put it back and close the hand.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
Six hours with picks and hot water and he comes up entire: a man of about thirty, dressed for weather, with a healed break in his forearm and four objects on him.
The fourth object is not of his century, or ours. It was in his coat, and his coat was made to hold it, and the coat is eleven thousand years old.

c.text:
The thaw runs in a strip two metres wide for four kilometres and ends at a mound, and the mound is not thawing at all: it is white with frost in the middle of a warm afternoon.
There is a door in it. There has always been a door in it. The thaw came from the door outwards, like something breathing on the ground.

choices.text: Open the door.
Put your ear to it first.

d.text:
It takes two of you to carry and it is worth every step.
The university in {region} pays out of a fund that exists for exactly this, and a woman from the Foundation is at the loading bay when you deliver it, and buys you a coffee, and asks four questions about what else was in the strip.

a1.text:
It is warm in your pack all the way home and it never cools.
Doesn't do anything else. That is the point: it does not do anything else, and eleven thousand years ago a man walked into a cold he could not survive rather than put it down.

a2.text:
You put it back and fold the fingers over it and pack the ice round the hand with your own hands until it is covered.
The thaw stops. Not slows: stops, in a ring around him, and the water that was running under the ground goes quiet.
What you take away is what was under the boat ribs, which the ground offers up while you are washing your hands.

c1.text:
It opens outwards, which is wrong for a mound, and the cold that comes out of it sits on you with real weight.
Inside there is a stair, and at the bottom of the stair there is a room with eleven thousand years of quiet in it and something in the middle of the quiet that has been waiting for the ground to soften.

c2.text:
Breathing. Slow: about one to your four. And under the breathing, a sound like somebody turning over in bed.
You back off, and you mark the mound on the map, and you take the news to the one office that will do anything with it, and they thank you in a way that suggests they knew, and pay you in a way that suggests they did not know it had started.

d_m.text:
It takes two of you to carry and it is worth every step, and the university in {region} pays out of a fund that exists for exactly this.
Then they clean it, which takes {three weeks|a month|some weeks}, and under the blade-work there is more blade-work, older, and under that a third layer, and the post has been recut {three times|twice|by three different hands} over what must be centuries.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Somebody kept re-carving it.|Three hands. Same post.|That is maintenance, not art.}"
asides.any: {member} {asks to see the cleaning photographs|writes down the order of the layers|reads the report twice}

choices.text: Take the money. It is their post now.
Read the oldest layer.
Go back and look for where it was standing.

d_old.text:
The oldest cut is not decoration and it is not a name. It is {an instruction|a warning|a set of directions}, and the two later hands have carved over the top of it without effacing it, which takes a particular kind of respect.
What it says is short and is about the mound at the end of the thaw, and it is not advice about how to open it.

d_site.text:
The hole the post stood in is still there and is {full of meltwater|open|not filled in}, and under the meltwater the packing stones are set in a pattern that goes on past the hole.
It is a line of them, and the line runs {four kilometres|a long way|straight} along the strip of thaw, and there are post holes in it every {ninety paces|hundred metres|so often}, and all of them are empty.

c2_m.text:
An ear on the door of the mound: breathing, slow, about one to your four, and under it a sound like somebody turning over in bed.
There is also, once the ear has been there {a minute|long enough|a while}, a second sound, and the second sound is {a door being tried|somebody at a handle|the latch moving} from the inside, patiently, at intervals, as though it has been tried a great many times.

choices.text: Back off and mark it for somebody else.
Hold the door shut and put something through the latch.
Knock.

c2_bar.text:
A bar through the latch, cold-set, hammered over at both ends with what is in the pack, which takes {an hour|the rest of the light|longer than anybody wants to stand there}.
The trying stops while the work is going on and starts again afterwards, at the same interval, against a door that will now not open. The party marks the mound for the Foundation and walks {four kilometres|the whole strip|back} with their ears ringing.

c2_knock.text:
Four knocks on a door in a mound in the middle of a thaw, because somebody in this party is the kind of person who knocks.
The breathing stops. Everything stops. Then the latch is tried once more, and there is a sound on the other side of the door that is unmistakably {a person sitting down|somebody sitting down|weight settling on a floor}, and after that it is quiet, and the door is not tried again while anybody is listening.

e_volcano.title: {The Vent|A Man Explaining That Lava Is Safe Now|Four Hundred Degrees And A Deckchair}

n0.text:
There is a deckchair at the lip of an active vent, and a man in it, in shorts, reading a newspaper, at a distance where the newspaper should be alight.
He has a cool box. He offers you a drink without looking up.
"It's been safe since the ritual," he says. "Nobody believes me. There's a radio programme about it."
The deckchair has been in that spot long enough to have {left marks|worn the rock|made its own two dents}.
n0.emText:
A deckchair at the lip of an active vent, and a man in it in shorts, reading, at a temperature that should have taken the paper off him.
"It's been safe since the ritual," he says. Since the ritual. That is your calendar he is using. Everything in this world dates itself from the night they took ninety-two per cent of you and made a spear out of it.
n0.bubba: Bubba is already in the second deckchair with a bottle from the man's cool box. "He's right, y'know. It's warm. It's real warm. Ma nun coce. Sit down, sugar."

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.cautious: {member} {watches the perimeter with a frown: "Bad idea."|checks their weapon charge and backs up a step|keeps a finger on the safety and mutters a warning|eyes the surroundings: "This has trap written all over it."}
asides.hedonistic: {member} takes the drink, sits on the ground, and declares this the best afternoon of the month.

choices.text: Sit down and have the drink.
Ask what happened during the ritual.
Go down into the vent.
Tell him to get away from the edge and mean it.

a.text:
You sit at the lip of a volcano in a deckchair and drink something cold, and the heat comes up past you and does not touch you, and it is the strangest twenty minutes of the season.
He talks. He has been doing this for four years. His wife thinks he is at work.

choices.text: Ask what he does down there.
Stay until dark.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
"Something came up and something went down," he says. "The mountain got quiet after. Not cold. Quiet."
He was here. He was one of the men on the emergency cordon on the thirty-first, and he has the photographs, and he keeps them in the cool box under the bottles, in a plastic bag, because that is where they are safest.

choices.text: Look at the photographs.
Buy the photographs.

c.text:
There are steps. Somebody cut steps.
Forty metres down it is bright and it is bearable and the air is wrong in the mouth, and there is a ledge, and on the ledge there are things left: tools, a boot, a wedding ring, a Foundation seal with the date scratched off, and a doorway in the rock with the heat going into it.

choices.text: Go through the doorway.
Take what is on the ledge and climb out.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

d.text:
He goes, because you said it like that, and he is furious about it, and halfway up the slope he stops being furious and starts shaking.
The safe zone ends four metres from where his deckchair was. You find that out by watching what happens to the deckchair when he takes it.

a1.text:
"Fetching," he says. "Fetching. There's a ledge. People leave things and other people want them."
He is a courier for a doorway in a volcano and he is paid in cash by four different offices. He will take you down as far as the ledge and no further, and he tells you exactly why not, and the reason is not fire.

a2.text:
After dark the vent glow lights him from underneath like a stage, and the mountain does something you will never be able to describe to anybody: it exhales, once, and the exhalation is shaped, and there are words in it that are not in any language and are unmistakably a greeting.
He waves back. He does it the way you wave at a neighbour.

b1.text:
Four photographs of the night of the thirty-first, taken from a cordon at the wrong angle, of a thing going down into a vent that is a great deal larger than the vent.
The fourth photograph has people in it. One of them is looking at the camera.
b1.emText:
Four photographs from the cordon on the thirty-first of December, 2001. Something enormous going down into a vent that is far too small for it.
In the fourth, at the edge of the frame, there is a woman on a stretcher with her eyes open, and you have never seen your own face from the outside on that night, and now you have.
b1.bubba: Bubba looks at the fourth one for a long time and then puts it face down. "Nah, sugar. Basta accussi'. Not today."

b2.text:
He will not sell them. He gives you one, the second, which is the least useful and the most beautiful, and asks you to show it to people.
You do. Four people laugh. The fifth pays enough to keep the whole party fed for a month and asks where the other three are.

c1.text:
Through the doorway the heat stops entirely, which the body reads as falling.
What is on the other side has been paid by everybody who has ever stood on that ledge and it is very interested in somebody who came through without leaving anything.

c2.text:
Tools, a boot, a ring and a seal. The ring is gold and the seal is worth four times the gold to the right buyer.
On the way up the steps you understand that you have taken payment off an altar, and that this is noted, and that it is not the sort of debt that gets collected quickly.

c2_m.text:
Tools, a boot, a ring and a seal, all of it on the ledge forty metres down where the air is wrong in the mouth and the light comes up from below.
The ledge is also swept. Not clean: {swept|brushed|kept}, with the dust pushed to one end in a line, and the tools are laid out in the order a person lays tools out when they intend to come back to them.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{That is a workbench.|Somebody works here. Today.|Do not take the tools.}"
asides.any: {member} {puts the ring back down|looks at the doorway rather than the ledge|counts the tools}

choices.text: Take the lot and climb out.
Take the seal and leave the tools.
Read the tools. Whose trade is this?

c2_seal.text:
The seal goes in the pocket and everything else stays exactly where it was lying, in its own order, on a swept ledge in a volcano.
On the way up the steps there is somebody coming down. They stand aside for each other on a cut stair {forty metres|a long way} down a vent, and neither says anything, and the party is a hundred metres up the slope before anybody breathes properly.

c2_tools.text:
They are not mining tools and they are not a mason's. They are {a smith's|a jeweller's|fine work} tools, for very small hot work, and two of them are for a job that does not exist in any trade anybody in the party can name.
Which means what is made on this ledge is made for whatever is through the doorway, and it is made {to order|to a pattern|to somebody's specification}, and the courier in the deckchair is the delivery end of a working business.

b1_m.text:
Four photographs of the night of the thirty-first, taken from a cordon at the wrong angle, of a thing going down into a vent that is {a great deal brighter|much brighter|lit} than it should have been.
In the fourth one there is somebody on the lip in the foreground, out of focus, in a deckchair, reading. The photographs are {forty years old|from the year of the ritual|old}, and the man in the chair beside the party is the man in the chair in the picture, at the same age.

choices.text: Say nothing about the fourth photograph.
Put it to him.
Ask to see the negatives.

b1_put.text:
He does not deny it and he does not explain it. He folds the newspaper, which he has not done all afternoon, and says that the mountain went quiet after the thirty-first and that somebody has to sit at the lip, and that it has been him since.
He would like it to stop being him. He says so once, clearly, and then unfolds the newspaper again, and that is the whole of the offer.

b1_neg.text:
The negatives are in a tin under the deckchair, which tells you how seriously he takes the possibility of the chair ever being moved.
On the negative the fourth frame has {more in it|a great deal more in it|something in the corner} than the print does, because the print was cropped, and what was cropped out is standing on the far lip, and there are {nine|eleven} of them.

e_ruins.title: {The Sunken Floor|A Room That Is Lower Than It Was|The House With Four Cellars}

n0.text:
Half a house, and the half that is left has a floor in it that has gone down: not collapsed, lowered, all in one piece, tiles unbroken, about a metre and a half below where the doorstep says it should be.
At the far side of the sunken floor there is a door that used to be a cellar door and is now at eye level, and it is shut, and it is newer than the house.
In the wallpaper, {sign}.
The lowered floor has gone down {evenly|level|by exactly the same amount all round}, which is not something a floor does when it fails.
n0.emText:
Half a house with its floor lowered a metre and a half, all in one piece, tiles unbroken, and a cellar door that is now at eye level and is newer than everything around it.
Something took a level of this building away and put a different one in. You know the trick from the inside. There is an entire floor of you missing and the door to it is at the wrong height too.
n0.bubba: Bubba drops down onto the tiles and stamps twice. "Solid. Uh-huh. Somebody built this here on a Tuesday, sugar, an' the house ain't from a Tuesday."

asides.artistic: {member} says the wallpaper pattern continues below the new floor level, which means the new floor is inside the old room.

choices.text: Open the cellar door.
Take the floor up.
Search the standing half of the house.
Knock. Properly. And wait.

a.text:
Behind it: a corridor, dry, plastered, lit by nothing you can identify, running further than the footprint of the house allows.
On the left-hand wall, at regular intervals, are doors, and each door has a number, and the numbers do not run in order, and the fourth one is your own house number, whichever of you is thinking about that.

choices.text: Open the numbered door that means something to somebody.
Walk the corridor to the end.

asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
The tiles come up in one piece each, laid on sand, and under the sand there is a second floor, and it is the original, and between the two there is a hand's width of space with things in it: a shoe, a comb, {paper}, a bundle of letters, a doll.
Everything that was on the old floor when it was lowered was swept into the gap first. Neatly.

c.text:
Two rooms and a stair to nowhere.
In the second room there is a table with a meal on it, four places, cutlery down, and a chair pulled out. The food is dust. The chair is not: the chair has been sat in this week, and the dust round it has been disturbed by a coat.

choices.text: Sit in the chair.
Lay a fifth place.

d.text:
You knock on a cellar door at eye level in a ruined house and you wait, and it takes a minute and a half, and then somebody knocks back: four knocks, evenly spaced, from a long way off, getting nearer with each one.
The fourth is on the other side of the door.

choices.text: Open it.
Say who you are through the door.

a1.text:
It opens on a room you know, and it is not this decade, and there are people in it who are not surprised to see you and do not stop what they are doing.
You are in there for four minutes. You come out with something that was on the sideboard, and with a headache, and a certainty about a thing you had chosen not to be certain about.

a2.text:
Four hundred metres, which the house does not have.
The end of the corridor is a wall with a bell push in it. Zero bell, there is no wire, and when you press it, somewhere behind you, in the ruin, a door opens.

c1.text:
The chair is warm. From the chair, the table looks laid rather than abandoned, and the room looks lit, and there is a fifth person in the doorway you cannot look at directly.
You are welcome. You are, quite clearly and quite kindly, welcome, and you are not being asked for anything, and that is the frightening part.

c2.text:
You set a fifth place with what is in the sideboard and you sit down and eat your own food at a dead table.
When you have finished, the fifth place has been used. Nobody saw it happen. Under the plate there is {relicWord} and a note in a hand nobody can read, and the pulled-out chair is pushed in.

d1.text:
The corridor is there and so is the person who knocked, and they are a metre and a half below you, standing in the old house at the old floor level, looking up.
They have been down there since the floor was put in. They are not asking to come out. They are asking whether it is still {timeAgo} up here.

d2.text:
You say your name and your business through a cellar door.
The answer comes back in your own voice, saying your name and your business, and then a second voice, saying: "Not that one. The other one. Send the other one."
Nobody opens the door. Everybody agrees, later, that this was correct.

b_m.text:
The tiles come up in one piece each, laid on sand, and under the sand there is a second floor, and it is the original.
Between the two there is {a hand's depth|a gap|room}, and in the gap, laid flat and spaced out on the lower floor, there are {nine|eleven} objects, one under every third tile, and none of them are valuable.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Nobody hides worthless things carefully.|Those are not hidden, they are placed.|One every third tile. That is a plan.}"
asides.any: {member} {numbers the tiles as they come up|leaves each object where it is and photographs it|counts to nine and then counts again}

choices.text: Lift them all and take the lot.
Work out what the spacing is for.
Put the tiles back down and leave it as it was.

b_space.text:
The spacing is not decoration and it is not storage: it is {ballast|packing|a level}, and each object has been chosen for its weight, and together they hold the upper floor exactly {level|true|square} on the sand.
Take one and the floor tilts. Take all nine and the floor goes down the rest of the way, and the rest of the way is a good deal further than the house has under it.

b_back.text:
Every tile back on its own bed of sand in its own place, which takes {four hours|the rest of the day|longer than lifting them did} and is done by people who have decided they would rather not find out.
The floor is level. It is still level {a year later|when anybody next passes|years after}, and the half-house is still standing, and nobody in the village can explain why that corner never falls.

d2_m.text:
You say your name and your business through a cellar door and the answer comes back in your own voice, saying your name and your business, {one word behind|a beat late|half a second after}.
Then it says a third thing, which you have not said, and which is a question, and the question is whether you are coming down or whether it should come up.

choices.text: Say nothing else. Leave the house.
Say: come up.
Answer in a language it has not heard you use.

d2_up.text:
The door opens by itself from the other side and the corridor is there and so is the step up, which is {a metre and a half|a good height|higher than it should be}.
What comes up is not in a hurry and is not hostile and is wearing a coat the party recognises. It stays {four minutes|a quarter of an hour|a while}, in the standing half of the house, and then goes back down, and the cellar door will not open again for anybody.

d2_lang.text:
A sentence in a language none of the party has spoken out loud in this country, said through a cellar door in a ruin, and the door does not answer it.
It cannot. Whatever is down there works from what it has heard, and it has just been shown the edge of that, and the knock that follows is {four knocks|different|a request rather than an echo}, and after that the arrangement between the party and the house is on an entirely different footing.

e_graveyard.title: {The Fresh Grave|Nobody Has Died Here Since {timeAgo}|Dug Last Night}

n0.text:
A country graveyard with nine hundred years in it and one grave dug last night: sharp edges, heaped spoil, no stone, no flowers, no notice on the gate.
The parish register in the porch says nobody has been buried here since {timeAgo}.
The hole is exactly the right size, and it is dug the way a professional digs, and there is a spade left in the spoil heap, which no professional would ever do.
The spade is left standing in the spoil at an angle that means somebody intends to come back to it {tonight|shortly|before morning}.
n0.emText:
One fresh grave in a nine-hundred-year churchyard, cut last night by somebody who knew the work, and a spade left standing in the spoil, which nobody who knows the work would do.
The hole is the right size for a person. You have a horrible and specific feeling about which person, and it is the same feeling you get looking at a doorway you cannot remember walking through.
n0.bubba: Bubba looks in the hole, then at you, then back in the hole. "Sugar, that's about your size. Nun me piace pe' niente. C'mon now."

asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
