choices.text: Get in the grave.
Wait for whoever comes back for the spade.
Fill it in.
Find the priest.

a.text:
It is deep enough that the sky is a rectangle and the church is gone.
The sides are cut clean. At the foot end, at about the depth of a knee, there is a niche cut into the earth, and there is something in the niche, wrapped, and it is the only reason this hole exists.

b.text:
They come back at dusk: a woman in her fifties with a wheelbarrow and a second spade, and she is not a gravedigger, she is a solicitor from {region}, and she has been digging her own family's graves for two years because the parish will not.
"There's nobody in any of them," she says. "That's the thing nobody will put in writing."

choices.text: Help her dig.
Ask what she is expecting to find.

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
It takes forty minutes and it is the right thing to do and everybody knows it.
At about the halfway point the spoil stops going in. It goes in and it is not there; the level does not rise. You are shovelling earth into a hole that is not accepting it, and the last of the light is going.

choices.text: {Keep going|Push deeper|Continue forward|Press on} until it is full.
Stop, and put the spade back where it was.

d.text:
The priest is in the vestry with the register pages in front of him, the four that were cut out, and a glass of something, and he is not surprised.
"It's the fourteenth," he says. "They dig one every so often and if you fill it in they dig another and if you leave it alone it fills itself and there is nothing in the rite for this, I have looked, I have written to the diocese."

choices.text: Ask what happened with the first thirteen.
Offer to sit up with the grave all night.

asides.nurturing: {member} takes the glass off him gently and puts the kettle on instead.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b1.text:
Two hours in the dark with a solicitor, opening a grave that is a hundred years old, and she is right: there is a coffin, and it is empty, and it has been empty since it went in, because the wood has never been under weight.
What is in it instead is a box of papers, and the papers are what her family has been paying for the silence of for a century.

b2.text:
"Nothing," she says. "That's what I'm expecting. I want to be able to say I've seen the nothing."
You sit with her until the light is gone and she talks about her brother, and at the end of it she gives you the second spade and {payment}, and drives home, and does not dig again.

c1.text:
You fill a hole that will not fill, in the dark, until the spoil heap is gone and the hole is exactly as deep as it was.
Then something takes hold of the spade from the other end and does not pull, just holds, the way somebody holds a door you are trying to shut.

c2.text:
You stop, and you put the spade back in the spoil at exactly the angle you found it, and you leave the churchyard by the gate rather than the wall.
In the morning the grave is filled and the turf is on and the grass has taken, and the sexton, who has not been out in a year, will not discuss it.

d1.text:
"Filled, dug, filled, dug, and after the ninth I stopped filling them."
The five he stopped filling are all in the north corner, all grassed over, all with grass a different green, and the priest has never once been able to bring himself to walk on it.
You walk on it. Something under it is very glad somebody finally did.

d2.text:
You sit up in a churchyard from dark to four with a flask and a priest who talks for the first two hours and sleeps for the last two.
At four the grave fills itself. It takes about a minute and it does it from the bottom, and there is a sound with it that is nearly a voice, and afterwards there is a stone that was not there, with a name on it, and the name is not anybody's yet.

a_m.text:
It is deep enough that the sky is a rectangle and the church is gone, and the sides are cut clean by somebody who has dug a great many of these.
At the foot end, at about the depth of a knee, there is {a hole|an opening|a gap in the cut} going sideways, and it has been dug from the other direction, and the spoil from it is not in this grave.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Somebody dug in. Not out. In.|The spoil went somewhere else.|That hole has a far end and we are at the near one.}"
asides.any: {member} {puts a lamp to the hole|measures it against an arm|does not put a hand in it}

choices.text: Reach in and see what is in there.
Work out where the far end comes up.
Get out of the grave and wait for the spade's owner.

a_far.text:
Bearing, distance, a bit of arithmetic in a grave by lamplight, and the far end comes up {under the north corner|in the north corner|at the five that were never filled}.
There is a hole there, in the turf, the same size, with the spoil from this grave heaped beside it. Something has been digging between the two for {a while|some time|longer than last night}, and it has been going in both directions.

d1_m.text:
"Filled, dug, filled, dug, and after the ninth I stopped filling them." He says it the way a man says a thing he has been waiting {four years|a long time|years} to say to somebody who is not in the parish.
The five he stopped filling are all in the north corner. He has the register pages here, the four that were cut out, and he has not shown them to the diocese, and he says why, and the reason is {good|better than anybody would expect|not what the party expected}.

choices.text: Go and look at the five in the north corner.
Read the four cut pages.
Tell him to send them to the diocese. Tonight.

d1_pages.text:
Four pages of a nine-hundred-year register, cut out with a blade, covering {eleven|nine} burials across {two hundred years|two centuries|a long span}, and every one of them is the same surname.
The surname is on the gate of the farm at the bottom of the lane. It is also, in the current generation, the woman with the wheelbarrow, and she does not know, and the priest has been carrying that on his own since {the spring|the bad winter|whenever it was}.

d1_send.text:
Telling a country priest to hand his own parish's worst secret to the diocese takes {an hour|most of the bottle|longer than anybody wants}, and it works because the argument made is a theological one and he cannot answer it.
He posts them himself in the morning. What comes back {four months|a season|eventually} is two men, a faculty, and permission to fill the five in the north corner, which is done properly, with the whole village there.

e_swamp.title: {The Chapel In The Water|Ankle Deep In Somebody's Nave|The Roof Is Still Above The Reeds}

n0.text:
The reeds part on a chapel roof. The rest of it is under, and the water is exactly waist deep in the doorway and stays waist deep all the way to the altar, which is not how water works in a building that is standing on a slope.
Candles have been lit in there. Recently. On a shelf above the waterline there are four, and two are still burning, and there is no way in but the way you came.
The water is waist deep in the doorway and waist deep at the altar, and the chapel {slopes|is on a slope|goes down} towards the altar.
n0.emText:
A chapel drowned to the roofline, the water exactly waist deep all the way to the altar regardless of the floor, and four candles on a shelf above the line with two of them still lit.
Somebody comes here and keeps a rule. Rules like that hold a place together the way a stitch holds a wound. You have about eight per cent of yourself and no stitches at all.
n0.bubba: Bubba wades in first, hat held up over his head like a man carrying a cake. "Aoh. Nun sta' fredda. Sugar, this water ain't cold. It oughta be cold."

asides.artistic: {member} says the reflection in the water is a beat behind, and then refuses to look at it again.
asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}

choices.text: Wade to the altar.
Wait outside for whoever lights the candles.
Go down. Look at the floor.
Take the candles and go.

a.text:
The altar is above the water by the thickness of a hand. On it: a bowl, a stone, and a photograph of a man in a suit that fitted him ten years ago, weighted down with a coin.
Under the water, all round the altar step, the floor is covered in coins. Thousands. Every one of them face up.

choices.text: Take a coin.
Add a coin.
Take the photograph.

asides.hedonistic: {member} is doing arithmetic about thousands of coins and not enjoying anybody's reaction.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
A woman comes at dusk in waders with four candles in a bread bag, and she does the whole thing without speaking: in, light, out, and on the way out she puts one hand flat on the door frame.
She has done this every week for eleven years. She was told to by somebody who is in the photograph on the altar.

choices.text: Ask her to teach you the rule.
Offer to take a week for her.

c.text:
You go under. The water is warm and clear and there is light from somewhere below.
The floor is a foot below your feet and it is tiled and it is dry: there is a skin on the underside of the water, and under the skin the chapel is a dry chapel with pews and a hymn board with numbers still on it, and somebody is sitting in the third row from the back.

d.text:
You take four candles out of a chapel, two of them burning, and the water follows you.
Not fast. It comes out of the door behind you at walking pace, keeps to waist height, and stays exactly with you for two kilometres through a swamp until somebody has the sense to put the candles down on a tussock.

a1.text:
The coin is silver and old and worth something, and taking it turns every other coin on that floor face down.
All of them. At once. With a sound like a very long word being said backwards.

a2.text:
You put your own coin on the altar face up and the water drops, all at once, by the width of a hand, all through the chapel.
On the floor by the altar step, uncovered, is {relicWord} that has been under water for a long time and is completely dry.

a3.text:
The photograph is dry and the coin holding it down is not.
When you lift it, the man in the suit that fitted him ten years ago is standing at the back of the chapel, waist deep, waiting to be asked something. He has been waiting eleven years and he is extremely patient.

c1_m.text:
Eleven years of a business's post on a landing mat: bank statements for an account that has been growing, four court letters, and a hand-addressed envelope that is not like the others.
The hand-addressed one is {this year's|recent|postmarked last month} and there is no stamp on it, which means it was put through that door by somebody standing on this landing.

choices.text: Take the lot and read it somewhere else.
Open the hand-addressed one here.
Read the bank statements properly.

c1_hand.text:
One sheet, no signature, four lines, and the four lines are addressed to whoever is standing on the landing rather than to the business.
They are also instructions, and they are courteous, and they concern the bulb. The party follows them or does not; either way, the landing is a different place after reading them and nobody suggests staying on it.

c1_bank.text:
The account has been receiving {the same amount|a standing order|one payment} every month for eleven years from a company that does not trade, and paying out one bill: {the electricity|power|the supply} for this building.
Somebody is paying, by standing order, to keep one bulb burning on a landing above a shop that has been bricked up. The company's registered address is {four streets|the next street|close}.

e_docks.title: {The Impound|Nobody Has Claimed It In Eleven Years|Berth Four}

n0.text:
At the far end of the impound, past the fishing boats with the tax owing, there is a vessel with no name, no port of registry and no rust.
The harbour office has it on the books as unclaimed since {timeAgo}. Nobody has been aboard. The fenders are new, and somebody replaces them, and the harbourmaster will tell you straight out that it is not him.
There is a gangway. It is down.
She is on {eleven|nine} fenders and every one of them is new.
n0.emText:
An unclaimed boat at the end of the impound with no name, no registry and no rust, eleven years on the books, and somebody replacing the fenders.
The gangway is down. Things with no name and no papers that nobody will claim: you have a professional interest. You are one.
n0.bubba: Bubba walks the length of her and whistles. "No rust. Aoh. Eleven years in salt water an' no rust. Chesta nun e' 'na varca, sugar."

choices.text: Go aboard.
Buy her at the unclaimed sale.
Watch the berth overnight.
Cut her loose and see what happens.

a.text:
Below decks she is dry, warm, and stocked: charts, tinned food, bunks made up, a stove laid ready and not lit.
The chart on the table is of this harbour, and there is a course pencilled off it, and the course leaves in about four hours on a tide that is not the tide today.

choices.text: Wait four hours and see.
Take the charts and go.
Light the stove.

b.text:
The unclaimed sale is a man in an office with a form and a rubber stamp, and the price is nothing, because nobody wants a boat with no papers.
He fills in the form. He gets to the field marked VESSEL NAME and stops, and sits back, and says: "Every eleven years somebody buys her. Every eleven years the form comes back from the registry blank."

choices.text: Buy her anyway and name her yourself.
Ask to see the eleven previous forms.

c.text:
At about three in the morning somebody comes down the quay with a bag of fenders and a splicing kit, and does an hour's careful work, and does not go aboard.
When they have finished they stand at the foot of the gangway for a while, the way people stand outside a house they used to live in, and then they go.

choices.text: Follow them.
Speak to them there, on the quay.

d.text:
She goes out on the ebb, slowly, with nobody aboard, and turns at the harbour mouth, correctly, the way a vessel turns under helm.
Then she comes back. She comes back to berth four and puts herself alongside, and the mooring lines go over the bollards without anybody throwing them, and the harbourmaster is standing next to you by then and neither of you says anything for a while.

a1.text:
Four hours. The tide does what the almanac says it will do and nothing happens.
At one minute past, the stove lights itself, and the compass swings, and the boat is under way in a harbour that has not moved, and out of the porthole the quay is there and going past.
You are at sea for eleven minutes and back alongside with what she went out to fetch.

a2.text:
Charts of four coasts with soundings that are not in any survey and a pencilled course between them that touches at eleven places.
They are worth money to a fishing fleet and a fortune to the Foundation, and one of the eleven places is somewhere you are going to want to go.

a3.text:
It lights first time on a match, on a stove that has not been lit in eleven years, and the cabin fills with the smell of somebody else's dinner.
All four of you eat aboard a boat nobody owns. It is the best meal of the month and everybody sleeps aboard and nobody dreams, and in the morning the bunks are made and the stove is cold and laid ready again.

b1.text:
You name her out loud on the quay with the form on the bonnet of a car, and the man from the office writes it in, and the registry, eleven weeks later, sends the papers back complete.
Nobody can explain that. He frames his copy. You have a boat.

b2.text:
Eleven forms in a folder, each with a buyer, each with a blank name field, and the eleventh buyer is a woman who is still alive and still in this town and has never once mentioned it to anybody.
She is delighted to be asked. She has been waiting eleven years for somebody to ask.

c1.text:
They walk two miles to a house on the hill with a light on in one window and a hospital bed visible through it.
The fenders are for her father. He was master of that boat. He has not spoken for four years and every time the fenders are changed he squeezes her hand.

c2.text:
She is not startled. She has been half hoping somebody would be there.
What she gives you, at three in the morning on a quay, is the key to a locker aboard that nobody else has ever opened, and the name of the boat, which she asks you to say out loud when you are aboard, because she cannot bring herself to.

a2_m.text:
Charts of four coasts with soundings that are not in any survey and a pencilled course between them that touches at eleven places.
The eleven places are not ports. Four of them are open water, and one of them is {this berth|where the party is standing|the impound}, and the pencil mark at that one is {fresh|newer than the rest|this year's}.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{She is on a run and this is a stop on it.|Somebody pencilled us in.|Eleven marks. Four of them in open water.}"
asides.any: {member} {lays the charts out in order|measures the legs|checks the dates in the margin}

choices.text: Roll them up and take them.
Work out what is at the four open-water marks.
Leave the charts and take the almanac instead.

a2_open.text:
Three of them are over {deeps|charted deeps|nothing at all}. The fourth is over a bank that is {four fathoms|shallow|not deep}, and the bank is not on the modern survey and is on a chart from {1903|before the war|a long time ago}, and on that chart it has a name.
The name is the name that is not painted on this boat's bow, and the party is the first crew in {eleven years|a long while|a very long time} to have both halves of that.

a2_alm.text:
The almanac is this year's, which is the strangest thing on the boat: somebody buys her a new one every January and works the tides in it in pencil, {a month ahead|in advance|right through to December}.
The workings are correct and they are in a hand that changes, over eleven years, from a young hand to an old one. The party takes it, leaves the charts, and the boat is still in the impound the next time anybody passes.

b1_m.text:
You name her out loud on the quay with the form on the bonnet of a car, and the man from the office writes it in, and the registry has a boat in it that it did not have this morning.
He then turns the folder round and shows the party something he has clearly decided in the last {four seconds|moment|minute} to show them: the eleven previous forms, all with the name field blank, and eleven buyers, and a column he has not filled in for any of them.

choices.text: Do not look at the column. Take the keys.
Read the column.
Ask why he is showing you.

b1_col.text:
The column is headed {DISPOSAL|OUTCOME|CLOSED} and it is blank because none of the eleven were ever disposed of: the boat came back into the impound {eleven times|every time|each time}, unclaimed, with no name on the bow and the fenders new.
He has been doing the paperwork on the same vessel for {nineteen years|two decades|most of his working life} and has never once been able to write in that column, and today, because somebody named her, he can.

b1_why.text:
Because the party is the first buyer who said a name out loud on the quay rather than writing one on the form, which he says as though it were obvious and which he has evidently been waiting {years|a very long time|his whole career} for somebody to do.
He gives them the folder. All eleven forms. It is not his to give and he gives it anyway and goes back into the office and shuts the door.

e_road.title: {The Wayside Shrine|Somebody Keeps The Flowers Fresh|Four Kilometres From Anywhere}

n0.text:
A shrine at the roadside: a niche, a photograph behind glass, plastic flowers and real ones, and a candle in a jar with a lid on so the wind cannot have it.
The real flowers are fresh. The road here is straight, sighted, wide and dry, and there is no reason on earth for anybody to have died on it, and the dates on the plaque are four.
Four, at the same spot, over eleven years.
The plaque has three names on it and room cut for {a fourth|more|one more}.
n0.emText:
A roadside shrine with fresh flowers, on a straight dry sighted road where there is no reason for anybody to have come off, and four dates on the plaque over eleven years.
The road is not the problem. Something at this exact spot takes one person every so often, and somebody local knows the interval well enough to keep the flowers going.
n0.bubba: Bubba counts the dates. "Four. An' they's all in the same month, sugar. Guarda ccà. Stesso mese."

asides.melancholic: {member} reads the photograph rather than the plaque and stays there a while.
asides.cautious: {member} {watches the perimeter with a frown: "Bad idea."|checks their weapon charge and backs up a step|keeps a finger on the safety and mutters a warning|eyes the surroundings: "This has trap written all over it."}

choices.text: Wait for whoever brings the flowers.
Walk the hundred metres slowly, looking at everything.
Drive it. Fast.
Light the candle and say something.

a.text:
She comes on foot from a farm track with flowers out of her own garden and a cloth to do the glass.
She has done it for eleven years and she was not related to any of the four. "You keep it lit," she says, "and it stays four."

choices.text: Ask what happens if it goes out.
Ask about the fourth one.

b.text:
A hundred metres of clean tarmac, and at about sixty there is a place where the road noise under your boots changes, and there is a smell of {smell}, and every one of you feels the pull of it: the exact, specific desire to be on the other side of the road.
It is four metres across. It's not visible. Four people have driven into it at speed.

choices.text: Stand in it.
Mark it, properly, with paint and posts.

c.text:
You get to about ninety and at sixty metres past the shrine the wheel goes light, and the road is on the wrong side, and everybody in the vehicle sees a different thing standing at the verge.
Somebody's hands are on the wheel and they are not the driver's hands, and whether you come out of it is decided in about a second and a half.

d.text:
You light a candle at a roadside shrine and say a name out loud, which is all anybody has ever wanted done at any shrine anywhere.
The pull at sixty metres is gone by the time you get back in the vehicle. It comes back within the week; the woman with the flowers tells you as much, later, with no drama at all.
But this week, on this road, nobody is going to be number five.

a1.text:
"It went out in the bad winter," she says, "and that's number four."
She has kept it going through weather, illness and a hospital stay she discharged herself from. She is seventy-eight. She would like, very much, to be able to stop, and she cannot see a way to.

choices.text: Take the shrine on.
Find out what is actually at sixty metres.

a2.text:
"Number four was the man who put the plaque up for the first three," she says.
He had worked out the interval. He had come out to be here on the day, with a camera, to see it. She has the camera. She has never had the film developed and she gives it to you and asks you to do it somewhere far away from here.

b1.text:
Four metres of road where the light is very slightly on a delay.
Standing in it, you can see the road as it was: unmetalled, a track, and a crowd on it, and something being brought along it at walking pace with everybody following.
When you step out you are holding something that was pressed into your hand by somebody in that crowd.

b2.text:
Four posts, a can of paint, and two hours' work, and any driver on that road now has a reason to lift off.
The council take the posts out in the spring. By then the county surveyor has been out to see why somebody marked it, and has stood at sixty metres himself, and has put in a request for a bend.

a1a.text:
It is flowers, a cloth, and a candle, once a week, four kilometres from anywhere, for as long as you are in this country.
She shows you how the jar goes so the wind cannot have it, and how the glass is done, and she cries when you take the cloth off her, and she is dead within the year and the shrine has five names on it and none of them are new.

c_m.text:
Ninety on a clean straight with the shrine coming up on the left, and at sixty metres past it the wheel goes light and the road is on the wrong side.
It lasts {four seconds|about four seconds|no time}. Everybody is still in the vehicle, it is still on the tarmac, and it is now stopped, sideways, {a hundred metres|some way|well} past the shrine with the engine running.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Do not do that again.|That is number four and we are sitting in it.|The road did that. Not the car.}"
asides.any: {member} {is out of the door and being sick on the verge|looks back at the shrine|turns the engine off}

choices.text: Drive on and do not talk about it.
Go back and walk the sixty metres.
Check the vehicle. All of it.

c_check.text:
Wheels, steering, tyres, and then the tyres again with a lamp, and it is all sound, and the tread on the near side front has {four seconds|a mark on it|a flat} worn into it that was not there this morning.
It is a flat spot the shape of a locked wheel, and nobody locked a wheel, and the mark is the same on the off side, and it is the only physical evidence anybody has ever brought off that sixty metres.

b2_m.text:
Four posts, a can of paint, and two hours' work, and any driver on that road now has a reason to lift off.
While the second post is going in, the ground at sixty metres gives {differently|the wrong way|like nothing else on that verge}, and what is under the topsoil is {tarmac|an old surface|a road} running at an angle to the one that is there now.

choices.text: Finish the posts. Leave the old surface alone.
Dig the old surface out and see where it goes.
Put a post through it.

b2_old.text:
It runs {at forty degrees|across|at an angle} to the modern road and it is unmetalled under the tar, and following it with a bar and a spade for {two hours|an afternoon|a long while} takes it to a gate that is not a gate any more.
On the modern map the two roads do not cross. On a map from {1911|before the war|a long time ago} they do, at exactly sixty metres past the shrine, and that crossroads had a name and the name is on the plaque.

b2_post.text:
The post goes through the old surface on the fourth blow and then goes in {all the way|a great deal further than it should|to the head} as though there were nothing under it at all.
It is not recoverable. The hole it leaves is {a hand's width|small|narrow} and does not fill, and the light at that point on the road stops being on a delay from that afternoon onward, which is either a repair or a wound.

e_beach.title: {The Wrack Line|What The Tide Has Sorted|Everything Above The Weed Is Arranged}

n0.text:
The wrack line is sorted.
Not washed up: sorted. Plastic with plastic, wood with wood, bone with bone, in bands running the whole length of the beach, and at the top of the beach a fourth band of things that do not go together at all except that every one of them belonged to somebody.
There are no footprints anywhere on the sand. The tide went out two hours ago.
There are {nine|eleven} bands and the fourth is the only one with things in it that belonged to somebody.
n0.emText:
The tide line is sorted into bands: plastic, wood, bone, and at the top a fourth band of things whose only shared quality is that each one belonged to a person.
Something came out of the water and did the filing. You can feel the patience in it. Whatever sorts a beach into categories is a mind, and a mind that works at low tide and does not leave footprints has had a long time to practise.
n0.bubba: Bubba walks the fourth band with his hands behind his back like a man in a gallery. "Watches. Rings. A little shoe. Uh. Sugar, chesto e' 'nu cimitero, nun e' 'na spiaggia."

asides.melancholic: {member} stops at the fourth band and does not walk any further along it.

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Take something from the fourth band.
Add something to the fourth band.
Wait for the tide and watch it work.
Break the bands. Kick them all together.

a.text:
You lift a watch out of the band and every gull on the beach turns its head.
The watch is going. It has been in the sea long enough to be a shell and it is going, and it is showing a time that is four hours off, and the four hours are in the wrong direction.

choices.text: Keep it and wear it.
Put it back, exactly where it was.

b.text:
You put something of yours in the band of things that belonged to somebody.
The beach does not react. But when you look back from the dune path, an hour later, your thing has been moved: it is in the band, correctly placed, between an object that is older than it and an object that is newer.
It has been filed. You have been filed.

c.text:
Six hours of waiting in the marram grass and then the tide is in and the sorting happens in the dark, in the last twenty minutes before the water turns.
It's not one thing. It is a great many small things working in a line, and they are not animals, and when they have finished they go back into the water together and the beach is filed and the sand is smooth.
One of them stays. It has found something it cannot categorise, and it would like help.

d.text:
It takes four minutes to ruin a day's work.
By the time you are at the top of the beach the bands are re-forming behind you, and by the time you are at the dune path they are done, and every single thing in the fourth band is now facing the dune path.
That night, at the camp, something is heard doing the same sorting to your packs.

a1.text: It keeps four hours' bad time for eleven days and then stops, and the moment it stops something comes up the beach to the camp to collect it, and it is quite prepared to take the arm as well.

a2.text:
You put it back in its slot and step away, and the tide, which is not due, comes up the beach four metres, once, over your boots, and goes back.
Where it touched, at the edge of the fourth band, there is now a thing that was not there. It's not from the fourth band. It is payment.

b_m.text:
Something of yours goes into the band of things that belonged to somebody, and the beach does not react, and the gulls do not turn.
When you look back from the top of the beach the fourth band has been {re-sorted|gone through|worked}, and your thing is not at the end of it where you left it, it is {in the middle|four along|placed}, between two objects that are the same age as each other and not the same age as it.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{It has been filed.|Sorted by something. Not by year.|Go and look at what it is sitting between.}"
asides.any: {member} {walks back down the beach on their own|counts along the band|looks at the two objects either side}

choices.text: Leave it. It is in the band now.
Work out what the fourth band is sorted by.
Take it back out.

b_sort.text:
Not by age, not by material, not by size. The fourth band is sorted by {how long the owner had it|how much it was used|wear}, and the party's object has been placed correctly to within {a year|months|a season}, by something that has never met its owner.
Which makes the band a record rather than a heap, and makes the beach {a clerk|an archive|somebody's system}, and makes the whole wrack line legible to anybody willing to read left to right.

b_take.text:
It comes out of the band {easily|without resistance|the way anything comes off a beach} and goes back in the pocket, and the walk to the top of the beach is a long one.
The band closes over the gap before anybody has got there. For {eleven days|a fortnight|some time} afterwards, everything any of the party puts down is found later {sorted|moved|placed in a line with other things}, indoors, in rooms nobody else has been in.

d_m.text:
Four minutes to ruin a day's work, kicking nine bands into one heap along a hundred metres of wrack line.
By the time anybody is at the top of the beach the bands are re-forming behind them, and they are re-forming {faster|much faster|at a pace nothing should manage}, and the fourth one is re-forming first.

choices.text: Keep walking. Let it come.
Go back and help it. Sort the fourth band properly.
Watch the re-forming and work out what is doing it.

d_help.text:
Four people on their knees on a cold beach at dusk putting a stranger's filing system back the way it was, which takes {three hours|until dark|considerably longer than kicking it over}.
It is not right. It is close. The gulls come back at some point and stand about watching without turning their heads, which is apparently the beach's way of accepting an apology, and nothing comes up to the camp that night.

d_watch.text:
It is not the tide and it is not the wind and it is not the gulls. It is the {sand|beach|ground} itself, moving each object {a hand's width|a little|a few centimetres} at a time in the intervals when nobody is looking directly at it.
Which is, it turns out, measurable, and the rate is constant, and the rate gives a date for when the sorting started, and the date is {this year|recent|inside the last twelve months}.

e_lake.title: {The Weir|The Water Goes Over And Does Not Come Back|Four Metres Of Missing River}

n0.text:
The lake drains over a weir into a river, and it should be the same amount of water on both sides, and it is not: the river below is about half what goes over the top.
The weir keeper's hut is padlocked from the inside. There is a gauge board in the water with the numbers painted on it, and somebody has repainted the numbers so they run the other way.
Under the weir, {sound}.
The gauge boards are painted backwards on both banks, and on both banks the paint is {fresh|less than a year old|newer than Tomas}.
n0.emText:
Half the water going over this weir does not come out the other side, and the gauge board has been repainted so the numbers run backwards, and the keeper's hut is padlocked from the inside.
Somewhere under this weir there is a hole in the world that takes water and does not give it back, and somebody local has adapted to it by relabelling the measuring stick, which is the most human thing you have seen all week.
n0.bubba: Bubba stands in the tailrace up to his knees and holds his hat out. "Sugar, half a river's goin' someplace. E' 'nu buco. Somewhere there's a town gettin' rained on indoors."

choices.text: Get into the hut.
Go under the weir.
Follow the missing water.
Ask in the nearest village about the gauge board.

a.text:
The window goes in easily. Inside: a bed, a stove, forty years of tide tables for a lake with no tide, and a man's coat on a hook.
The padlock is on the inside of the door and the key is in the lock. Zero other way out and there is nobody in the hut.

choices.text: Read the tide tables.
Wait in the hut for the keeper.

b.text:
Under the sheet of falling water there is a ledge, and past the ledge there is a doorway in the weir's own stonework, and the missing half of the river is going into it and not making any noise at all.
It goes down. It goes down a long way and the light goes with it.

c.text:
You follow it by finding where it comes out, which takes two days and four wrong guesses and one very good idea about wells.
It comes out eleven kilometres away, in a cellar, into a stone tank that is always exactly the same level, in a house that has been in the same family for four hundred years and has never once been short of water.

choices.text: Knock on the door.
Tell the water board.

d.text:
"Old Tomas did that," they say, in the bar, without being pressed. "Painted them backwards in the eighties. Said the lake was going the other way and somebody had better be counting it right."
Then the room goes quiet for a moment and somebody changes the subject with real skill, and you have to buy four rounds to get back to it.

choices.text: Buy the four rounds.
Ask where Tomas is now.

a1.text:
Forty years of a lake's levels, taken twice a day by hand, and in the last four years the numbers stop being levels and start being a countdown.
It reaches zero in eleven weeks. Underneath the last entry, in different ink: "Locked in. Do not open. It comes up the tailrace."

a2.text:
You sit in a weir keeper's hut until dark, and at dark the water noise changes, and something comes up the tailrace and tries the door.
It tries the door for eleven minutes. It's not strong. It is only extremely persistent, and it knows the door opens inwards, and it knows about the padlock, and it is disappointed that the padlock is done up.

c1.text:
The family are hospitable and completely unembarrassed. They have known for four hundred years. There is a paper about it, signed by an abbot, and an obligation attached, and they have kept the obligation every year without fail.
They are getting old. There is nobody after them. They would like to know if the party would consider the obligation, and they explain exactly what it involves before asking.

c2.text:
The water board send an engineer who takes one look at the tank, says a word you do not expect from an engineer, and files a report that goes to four offices and disappears in all four.
He pays for your drinks himself, out of his own pocket, and thanks you, and tells you what happened to the last man who filed one.

d1.text:
Four rounds gets you the whole thing: the count, the countdown, the eleven weeks, and the fact that the whole village knows and has decided, collectively, without a meeting, to be somewhere else that month.
They have been packing for two years. They show you the arrangements. They are extremely well organised and nobody has said it out loud once.

d2.text:
"In the hut," they say. "Where else would he be?"
It has been eleven years. Nobody has been in. Nobody has taken him a meal in eleven years and nobody thinks this is strange, and when you point out that a man cannot be in a hut for eleven years, they agree with you completely and go back to their drinks.

c2_m.text:
The water board send an engineer who takes one look at the tank, says a word you do not expect from an engineer, and goes back to the van for a torch.
He is down there {forty minutes|a long time|the better part of an hour}. When he comes up he is not writing anything, which for a man with a clipboard is a decision, and he asks the party, quietly, how much of it they saw.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{He is deciding whether to file.|That is a man working out what he can afford to have seen.|Watch what he writes.}"
asides.any: {member} {holds the torch|waits|does not answer straight away}

choices.text: Say: all of it. Let him file what he likes.
Say: nothing. Let him close it.
Look at his file number and follow it up yourself.

c2_shut.text:
He files it as a {blockage|structural query|routine defect} and the tank is sealed and grouted inside the fortnight, by a contractor, at night, and the river below the weir is the same amount of water as the lake above it from that week onward.
He posts the party {payment} in cash from his own money {four months|a season|some time} later with no note, which is either gratitude or a down payment on their silence and is probably both.

c2_file.text:
The file number is on the clipboard and the file is public, and pulling it takes {two afternoons|a fortnight|some persistence} and a request in writing.
There are {nine|eleven} of them for this catchment going back to {1954|the fifties|a long way}, all with different engineers' names, all closed as routine defects, all with the same paragraph typed in the same words. Somebody has been closing this for {fifty years|half a century|a very long time}.

d2_m.text:
"In the hut," they say. "Where else would he be?" It has been eleven years. Nobody has been in. Nobody has taken him a meal.
They are not being cruel about it, which is the strange part: the bar talks about Tomas in the present tense and has {a chair|his chair|a place} that nobody sits in, and somebody buys him a drink on a Friday and the glass is left on the bar.

choices.text: Go up to the hut and open it.
Buy him a drink and leave it on the bar.
Ask, carefully, when they last saw him.

d2_drink.text:
A drink bought for a man nobody has seen in eleven years, left on the bar in the right glass, which the landlord pours without being told which one.
It is gone at closing and the glass is on the shelf. Whatever else that means, it means the party has been accepted by that bar in a way that takes most people {years|a lifetime|generations}, and what comes out of the rest of that evening is worth going back for.

d2_seen.text:
The answer, once four people have stopped giving the easy version, is {last week|Tuesday|recently}, and the answer before that is that he comes down on a bicycle for the paint, twice a year, and pays cash.
He has been dead {eleven years|since the bad winter|a long time} by the parish register, which the party checks, and the register is not wrong, and neither is the bar.

e_wayside.title: {The Marker|A Stone With The Wrong Number On It|Nine Kilometres To Nowhere}

n0.text:
A milestone at the side of the track, cut, painted, maintained, with a place name on it and a distance.
The distance is nine. It was nine an hour ago at the last one, and it will be nine at the next, and the place it names is not on your map or on anybody's.
Somebody paints these. There is a paint tin in the grass behind it with the lid on properly.
The paint on every stone is the same age, which means they are all done on the same day, which means somebody does {nine kilometres|the whole run|all four} in an afternoon.
n0.emText:
A milestone that says nine kilometres to a place that is not on any map, and it said nine at the last one, and it will say nine at the next.
Somebody keeps the paint fresh. In your experience, the things that get maintained are the things that are still in use.
n0.bubba: Bubba shakes the paint tin. "Half full. Fresh. Aoh. Sugar, 'o pittore sta' vicino."

choices.text: Walk towards it.
Wait for whoever paints the stones.
Repaint the stone with the right number.
Note it, and go on.

a.text:
Nine kilometres of good track, four milestones, all of them nine.
At the fourth there is a bench and a view and a man sitting on it with a flask, who nods at you as if you were expected and says: "It's always nine. That's not a fault. That's the distance."

choices.text: Sit down with him.
Keep walking anyway.

b.text:
It takes until evening. He is about seventy, on a bicycle, with a brush and a rag, and he does the stone in four minutes and does not repaint the number, only the letters.
"The number's right," he says, when you ask. "It's the name people can't do."

c.text:
You paint a number on a stone that has had the same number on it for two hundred years, and the paint takes, and the track ahead of you is now four kilometres shorter and it arrives somewhere.
Where it arrives is a farm, with a family, and a dog, and a woman in the yard who drops what she is holding when she sees the track come out of the trees, because it has not come out of the trees in her lifetime.

d.text:
You write it down, because that is what a party with any sense does, and you go on.
The entry in the book is worth something to a man in {region} who collects exactly this, and he pays for it, and asks whether the paint tin had the lid on.
It did. He nods as if that settled something.

a1.text:
Flask tea on a bench with a view of nothing in particular, and an hour of a man who has been sitting at the fourth stone for a long time.
He explains the nine. It takes four minutes and it is entirely satisfactory and none of you can repeat it afterwards, and everybody feels considerably better for having heard it.

a2.text:
Four more stones, all nine, and the light going, and the track getting better rather than worse the further you go, which is the wrong way round.
At the ninth stone the track ends at a gate in a wall, and on the gate there is a bell, and the bell has a rope, and the rope is the only thing out here that is not maintained.

b_m.text:
It takes until evening. He is about seventy, on a bicycle, with a brush and a rag, and he does the stone in four minutes and does not look up until it is done.
Then he does look up, and he is not startled, and he says: "You have not walked it, then." He says it as a fact and as a kindness and it is not clear which of those is meant to hurt.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{He has met people like us before.|That is a man on a schedule.|Ask him what is at the ninth kilometre.}"
asides.any: {member} {holds the bicycle|looks at the wet nine on the stone|asks if he wants a hand}

choices.text: Talk to him at the stone.
Ask him why the number never changes.
Do the next stone for him.

b_why.text:
Because it is not a distance, he says, and then explains what it is, and the explanation is {four sentences|short|not long} and is entirely coherent and takes about a minute to become horrible.
The number is a count, the count is of something that has not happened yet, and the painting is what keeps it at nine. It has been at nine since {his father|the war|before he took it on}.

b_paint.text:
One stone, four minutes, with his brush and his rag and him watching from the saddle without comment.
He checks it afterwards, properly, with a thumb on the edge of the nine, and then says thank you and gives the party {the rag|his rag|the tin}, which is a thing he has evidently thought about for {some time|years|a while}, and rides off before anybody can decline it.

d_m.text:
You write it down, because that is what a party with any sense does, and you go on, and the entry in the book is worth something to somebody.
Four kilometres further on there is another stone, and it says nine, and the track behind is {visibly|obviously|by any measure} longer than nine kilometres and the party has been walking away from the place name the whole time.

choices.text: Keep going. Write down the second one too.
Turn round and walk back to the first stone.
Pace the distance between the two stones exactly.

d_back.text:
Walking back to the first stone takes {four kilometres|an hour|the same as it took}, and it is not there, and the track behind is {empty|clean|unmarked} for as far as anybody wants to keep looking.
The second one is still ahead of them when they turn round again, which is the wrong direction for it to be in, and it still says nine.

d_pace.text:
Paced properly, out and back, twice, the gap between the two stones is {three thousand nine hundred|not four kilometres|three point nine} paces, and the second measurement disagrees with the first by exactly nine.
So does the third. The error is not an error, it is {a rate|a constant|an interest}, and a party with an entry in a book and a number like that has something a cartographer will pay real money for.

e_camp.title: {The Cold Camp|Somebody Stopped Here Last Night|Four Cups, Three Drunk}

n0.text:
A camp, cold, from last night: fire ring, four cups, three of them drunk, and one full and covered with a saucer.
The kit is all here. Two packs, a bedroll rolled, a coat over a branch, a pair of boots side by side and pointed at the fire the way you point boots when you intend to put them back on.
Nothing has been dragged. Nothing has been taken. There are no tracks out.
Three cups are drunk to the leaves and the leaves are {dry|not wet|a week dry}, and the fourth is under a saucer.
n0.emText:
A cold camp from last night with four cups, three drunk and one covered with a saucer, and the boots pointed at the fire the way you leave boots when you are coming back to them.
Everything here says they intended to come back and nothing says they left. That is your whole biography in a fire ring.
n0.bubba: Bubba crouches by the fourth cup and does not lift the saucer. "Covered up. That's for somebody. Aspettavano a quaccheduno."

Go through the packs.
Make your own camp here and light the fire again.
Drink the fourth cup.

a.text:
Under the saucer the tea is hot.
Not warm. Hot, with steam on the underside of the china, in a cup that has been sitting in a cold fire ring since last night.
The moment the saucer is off, everything in the camp is a degree or two warmer, and somewhere behind you in the scrub something puts weight on a foot.

choices.text: Put the saucer back.
Leave it off and wait.

b.text:
Two packs: a woman's and a boy's. A permit for something else entirely, four letters home unposted, a map with a route on it that ends here and does not go on, and a photograph of four people at a fire ring.
The photograph is of this fire ring. There are four in it and two packs, which does not add up until you count again and notice that two of the four are wearing the same coat.

c.text:
You build the fire back up in somebody else's ring and cook, and eat, and sit, and the evening is one of the good ones: no wind, a clear sky, and something in the arrangement of the place that makes everybody talk more than usual.
At about four in the morning the fourth cup is empty and the saucer is stacked on the other three, washed.

d.text:
It is very good tea, and it is hot, and it is somebody's.
What comes to collect the cup does not want the cup back. It wants to know why you thought it was for you, and it asks in a way that does not use language, and it asks four times.

a1.text:
You put it back exactly as it was and the camp cools and the thing in the scrub takes its weight off the foot and everything is ordinary.
You leave the camp as you found it, and mark the position, and report it in {region} where somebody at a desk goes quite still and asks you to repeat the bit about the saucer.
They have four other reports. All four with a saucer.

a2.text:
Forty minutes, sitting in a cold camp with a hot cup of tea in the middle of it, and then they come back for their kit: two of them, a woman and a boy, walking in out of the scrub from a direction that has nothing in it.
They are perfectly all right. They have been gone one night. They have been gone, as far as anybody else is concerned, since {timeAgo}, and they are extremely keen to know what the party is doing at their fire.

b_m.text:
Two packs: a woman's and a boy's. A permit for something else entirely, four letters home unposted, a map with a route on it that does not go where the permit says.
The route ends {four kilometres|not far|a morning's walk} from here at a spot that is marked with a cross and a time, and the time is {this morning|today|two hours ago}.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{They are not lost. They had an appointment.|Somebody went to meet something at eight o'clock.|That is a rendezvous, not a route.}"
asides.any: {member} {folds the map and puts it in a pocket|reads one of the letters and puts it back|looks at the time and then at the sun}

choices.text: Take the useful kit and go.
Walk the route to the cross.
Post the four letters.

b_cross.text:
Four kilometres on a bearing off somebody else's map, and the cross is a {hollow|dip|place where the ground goes down} with a flat stone in it and two sets of boot prints going in.
One set comes out. It is the boy's, and it goes {east|the wrong way|away from the camp}, at a run, and it is {two hours|this morning's|recent}, and it is followable.

b_lost.text:
Four kilometres on a bearing taken off a sketch map in a hurry is {three kilometres|four kilometres|a walk} in the wrong direction, and the ground all looks the same, and the light goes.
The party gets back to the camp at {ten|dark|some hour} with nothing, and the fourth cup is cold, and the saucer is on the ground beside it, and nobody in the party put it there.

b_post.text:
Four letters, stamped at {the next town|the first post office|a village four hours on} out of the party's own money, and put in a box, which is the smallest possible act and takes about ninety seconds.
Two of them are answered, {months later|eventually|in the spring}, care of a poste restante the party never gave anybody. The answers are addressed to the woman and the boy. Both of them start: {"We got your letter"|"Thank God"|"We had given up"}.

c_m.text:
The fire goes back up in somebody else's ring and the evening is one of the good ones: no wind, food, and the country going dark politely around four people who did not have to walk any further today.
At about {eleven|midnight|the hour everybody stops talking} the fire does something it should not: it {goes green|burns green for a moment|changes colour} for about four seconds, all the way through, and then does not do it again.

choices.text: Nobody mentions it. Sleep well.
Put the fourth cup on the fire.
Work out what is in the ring.

c_cup.text:
A full cup of somebody else's tea, poured onto a fire that is not yours, in the middle of the night, by somebody who has decided to find out.
The fire goes out. All of it, instantly, including the embers, including the heat in the stones. The rest of the night is {very cold|extremely cold|as cold as it gets} and in the morning the ring is full of clean dry ash and the saucer is in the middle of it, unmarked.

c_ring.text:
The stones of the ring are river stone and one of them is not: it is {worked|cut|shaped}, set at the {north|upstream} point, and it has been in a fire a great many more times than this ring has been used.
It is also the reason the fire went green, and the reason it burned that well, and it is portable, and whoever laid this camp knew to put it in the ring and knew to leave it there.

"Two lanes at {lane}," they say. "Six o'clock. Bring your people. I've paid for the shoes."

d2_round.text:

Whoever is in the house at the top has been driving a line round this place for four years. The party can keep driving it, or they can hand the keys back, and both of those are answers.

He does it on the next lap. The car goes {four hundred metres|a long way|most of a straight} on its own momentum and comes to rest on the verge, and everything after that is a man being helped out of a car by eleven people who have been waiting since Tuesday.

e_ocean_fisher.title: {The Catch Nobody Will Buy|Three Men And A Full Hold|Every Fish Facing You}

n0.text:
There is a boat lying to out here with three men on it and none of them working.
The hold is full. That is the problem. They will not put in with it, they will not tip it back, and they have been out here {two|three|five} days deciding. The skipper, {trade}'s brother by the look of him, waves you alongside like a man waving down a bus.
"You know anything about fish," he says. It's not a question.
The net is inboard and stowed and {dry|bone dry|not wet}, and the hold is full.
n0.emText:
Three men, one boat, a full hold, and a stillness on the water that you recognise from the inside of your own head: the stillness of people who have made a decision they cannot say out loud.
The skipper waves you alongside like a man flagging a bus in a dream. "You know anything about fish," he says, and the water under his hull is exactly, unnaturally flat, the way things go flat around you when the eight per cent that came back starts paying attention.

He has {thirty-one years|three decades|a lifetime} of questions and answers in a notebook and no idea what to do with it, and he has been waiting for somebody who would not laugh, and the party is not laughing.

The level stops {a finger|an inch|just} below the lowest old mark. The old man says nothing at all, sets the chair back up, sits down, and casts, and after a while says that it has answered and that the answer was yes.

The last four are not years. The party is standing knee deep reading them when the water starts coming back up, which nobody has opened anything to cause.

They have been here since first light. The set comes in every twenty minutes, six waves, textbook, the kind of wave people move country for, and every one of them sits on the sand and watches it.

The break has not been there {a year|two seasons|long}, and there is no reef under it on any chart.
n0.emText:
A textbook break, eleven surfers on the sand, and none of them in the water. Six waves a set, every twenty minutes, and a rule about the sixth.
"Nobody rides the sixth," says a girl with an unwaxed board, and the sea behind her is keeping perfect time, and things that keep perfect time in this world are almost always keeping it for somebody.

He is at home, and he is fine, and he makes tea and talks about the break like a man describing a job he used to have.
The only thing wrong with him is that he does not go near the water and cannot say why, and that {every clock in the house|the kitchen clock|all four clocks} is four minutes fast, and he says he cannot get them to hold time and has stopped trying.

b_fine.text:
Fine means he came out of the water {four minutes|a few minutes|some time} after he went under, in front of eleven witnesses, having been under for {forty minutes|much longer than that|most of an hour}.
All eleven of them agree about that. None of them will say it to a stranger, and she has just said it, and she is {crying|not crying|very steady} and asks the party not to make her say it twice.

d_m.text:
Eleven surfers, a fire in an oil drum, four sets an hour and nobody in the water: it is the most peaceful afternoon anybody has had in months.
At about {five|the turn of the tide|four} the sixth wave of a set comes through, and every one of the eleven stands up at the same time without saying anything, and watches it all the way in.

choices.text: Watch it with them and stay on the sand.

Get in the water for the next one.

d_see.text:
Asked while they are all still standing, they answer honestly, because standing up has already admitted it: they see somebody in the face of the sixth wave, every set, every day, since the break arrived.
Not the same somebody. Each of the eleven sees {a different one|somebody of their own|a person they know}, and two of them have compared notes and stopped comparing notes, and the party is the first outsider to be told.

n0.emText:
Four hundred pallets of Collective water on a quay, under seal, under a guard who is asleep at four in the afternoon.
Everything else in this world is cut with something. The water is the one thing they sell straight, which is why they own all of it. Pallet four hundred does not move with the rest, and things that do not move with the rest are, in this world, either sacred or evidence.

The eleventh photograph is of the pallet label, and the label has a consignor on it, and the consignor is not the Collective. It is {a hospital|a research institute|a name with no address}, and the seal was put on afterwards.

a2_trace.text:
The consignor has no address and does have a bank, and the bank has a correspondent, and the correspondent has {four|five} other consignments on the same account, and all of them are pallets of bottled water, and all of them are under Collective seals.
Which is {four hundred thousand|a great many|a very large number of} bottles that are not what the label says, in {four|five} countries, and the party has the account number.

a2_coll.text:
The Collective's own people are {four hours|a day|not long} away and are considerably more alarmed than the party expects, because a forged seal is worse to them than whatever is in the pallet.
They pay for the photographs, generously, and for silence, less generously, and the pallet is gone from the quay by morning and so is the guard who was on it, and nothing is ever said about the consignor.

b2_m.text:
Two men in a hire car, on the Thursday, with a hand-held meter and a clipboard. They do not open the pallet. They {walk round it|hold the meter against it|take a reading} and write, and get back in the car.
The meter is not a meter anybody in the party recognises and the clipboard is a printed form with {four hundred|a great many} lines on it, and most of the lines are filled in.

b2_form.text:
Four hundred lines, one per pallet, with a reading against each and a column at the right headed {with one letter|by a single character|with a symbol}, and pallet four hundred's entry in that column is the only one that is not blank.
The readings on the other three hundred and ninety-nine are all the same number. Four hundred's is not, and it has been going up, fortnight by fortnight, for eleven months.

b2_caught.text:
The clipboard is held by a man who has been holding clipboards professionally for {twenty years|a long time|his whole working life} and who does not turn round so much as stop.
Nothing is said. The party is photographed, from the hire car, twice, on the way off the quay, and the following week there is a man at the end of whichever street they are staying on, and there is one the week after that too.

b2_follow.text:
The hire car does {four|five} more quays in two days, at a steady pace, and ends at a unit on an industrial estate in {region} with no sign on it and a good lock.
What is in the unit is {three hundred and ninety-nine|the rest of them|every other pallet on the form}, stacked, sealed, being read fortnightly by two men with a meter, and one empty space at the end of the row that is the size of pallet four hundred.

e_fields_pigeon.title: {The Loft With The Door Left Open|Forty Birds And A Shoebox|Thursday's Post}

n0.text:
A pigeon loft in the corner of a field, painted the same green as everything the council ever painted, door swinging.
Inside: forty birds, fed and watered, and one girl of about nine sitting on an upturned crate with a shoebox on her knees, doing the accounts of somebody else's business in a school exercise book.
"You're late," she says, without looking up. "He said two people. There's {two|three|four} of you."
The loft door swings and the birds do not leave, which is not how a loft with the door open works.
n0.emText:
A pigeon loft, door swinging, forty birds all fed. A girl of about nine on a crate with a shoebox and an exercise book, running an operation.
"You're late," she says. "He said two people." You have been alive, as far as you can prove, for eleven months, and a nine-year-old has your appointment written down. Somewhere in the ninety-two per cent, you suspect, you were also somebody's appointment.
n0.bubba: Bubba crouches down to her level, which takes some doing. "Ma' guagliona, who's he? Talk to me. I'm the money." He is not the money.

b1_leave.text:
It can, she says, but not by them and not here: {a smallholding|this ground|a place with goats on it} is the wrong place to ask anything to leave, because things that are asked to leave have to have somewhere to go.
What she does instead is tell the party how to ask, and where, and what it costs, and the cost is not money and is not large and is the kind of thing that only becomes expensive years later.

n0.emText:
A line surveyor with her kit packed and her hands round a mug. "Nothing casts here," she says. "Hasn't since the eighties."
You can feel it: the ley runs under this col and it is broken the way a bone is broken, and the whole mountain is holding the limb still. You are made of a break like this. Yours went the other way: everything poured out of you and something enormous poured in.

b1_back.text:
Standing in eleven metres of somewhere else a second time, deliberately, to give something back, is a decision that nobody in the party argues with and everybody remembers.
It is taken. The break {closes|narrows|goes} by about a metre while everyone is watching, which is the first time in six years it has done anything except widen, and the surveyor writes that down with her hands shaking.

b1_bear.text:

It reads. It reads a direction and a distance, and the distance is {four hundred kilometres|a long way|off this mountain entirely}, and at the other end of it there is a second break that nobody has ever found and that is now on a chart.

While it is going through, the surveyor is {moved on|reassigned|taken off the mountain}, and her notebooks are requested by a firm of solicitors acting for a client who is not named, and she rings the party from a call box to ask what to do.

choices.text: Tell her to hand them over. It is published now.

d1_lodge.text:

a2_m.text:
He comes out with you at the hooter, over the chalk, holding your arm, and on the outside he stands still for a very long time and looks at the sky.
He lasts nine days. On the fourth of them he tells the party something he has been carrying since {Tuesday|the day it closed|whenever it was}: that there is a man in there who came in {after|later than the rest|three years after it shut}, on purpose, and who knows how.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Somebody walked in voluntarily.|If he got in after it closed he knows the way.|Nine days. Ask him everything.}"
asides.any: {member} {writes down everything he says|sits with him|asks which man}

choices.text: Let him have his nine days in peace.
Get the name of the man who walked in.
Go back to the line and shout for him.

a2_name.text:
The name comes with an address, a trade and a reason, and the reason is {his daughter|somebody in there|one of the forty}.
He went in in {1987|the third year|a long time after the hooter} carrying a crowbar and a bag of food that would not have lasted an afternoon, and he is in there now, four minutes at a time, and the party can see him from the rim if they know which shift he is on.

c2_m.text:
Eleven years of observations at four minute eleven second intervals, in eleven notebooks, all of it methodical, all of it in the same hand.
She will sell them. She names a price that is {far too low|almost nothing|a month's rent} and then, while the money is being counted, says that there is a twelfth notebook and that it is not for sale and is not about the quarry.

choices.text: Buy the eleven. Leave the twelfth.
Ask what is in the twelfth.
Buy nothing. Offer to take the observations over for a season.

c2_twelve.text:
It is about the caravan. Eleven years on a rim with binoculars is eleven years of somebody being on the outside of a bubble, and the twelfth notebook is where she has been writing down {what she has noticed about herself|the four minute gaps in her own days|the things that do not add up out here}.
There are {nine|eleven} of them. She reads two out. Then she puts the kettle on and does not read any more, and the party does not ask.

c2_take.text:
A season of four minute eleven second intervals on a rim in a caravan, in shifts, with a borrowed pair of binoculars, so that she can go down into the town and sleep in a bed and see a doctor.
She comes back after {a month|five weeks|six weeks} looking like a different person. The notebooks stay hers. The party's shifts are in them, in a second hand, and she has annotated every one of them with corrections.

e_ruins_ghost.title: {The Spectral Auditor|Ghost With A Grudge|Unfinished Business}

n0.emText:
Something's crossing the ruins in a dead straight line, in a court usher's coat, with a paper in its hand, at the pace of a functionary.
Eris's court fetches people like this. She is not going to be fetching you. She has other arrangements for you, and they are worse, and they involve being invited.
n0.bubba: Bubba goes very still. "Aoh. That's a summons walkin'. Sugar, listen to me: it ain't for me an' it ain't for you. 'A carta e' pe' n'atu."

asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.brave: {member} {steps up front with a weapon ready: "I'll take point."|grins and racks the slide: "Let's see what wants to die today."|is already at the hatch before anyone can argue|steps over the threshold without flinching}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: {Show him a fake permit from your pocket|Bluff your way past the ghost|Flash a forged municipal pass|Argue zoning law with him}
{Tell him the government collapsed two centuries ago|Break the news about the empire|Inform him his department got liquidated|Laugh at his imaginary fines}
{Grab whatever shiny relics he's guarding and bolt|Loot the altar while he rants|Snatch the grimorie and run|Ignore him and loot the chest}
{Draw steel on the officer|Put the usher down|Cut the clerk out of the air|Swing at him and be done}

a.text:
It walks into you and stops, exactly, at contact, and looks up for the first time.
It has a face like a passport photograph of somebody who has been dead a while. It waits. It is waiting for you to say the thing that people say to an usher, and none of you knows the thing.

choices.text: Say you are not the one it wants.
Say you will come.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
It goes to a cellar under the third heap and stands at the top of the steps and reads out a name, once, and waits.
The name is answered. Somebody comes up out of that cellar who has been living down there, and they are shaking, and they go with it, and neither of them looks back at you.

choices.text: Go down into the cellar they came out of.
Walk with them as far as they will let you.

c.text:
It lets you. That is the thing nobody expects: it holds the paper out, patiently, like a man showing a ticket.
It is a summons out of the Court of Eris, in four languages, three of which are not used for paperwork, and the name on it has been struck out and rewritten twice. The second name is not the one it read out at the cellar.

choices.text: Add a name.
Hand it back and let it get on with its work.

d.text:
You put a court officer down in a field of rubble, which is a thing that can be done and which has consequences.
It comes apart like a coat falling off a hook. The paper does not. The paper stays in the air where its hand was, and then goes, on the same bearing, at the same pace, without it.

a1.text:
"I am not the one you want."
It looks at the paper. It looks at you. It compares, visibly, for about eight seconds, and then it steps round you, which is the first time it has deviated from the line, and goes on.
Where it stepped round you, the ground is scorched in two footprints, and there is something in the scorch.

a2.text:
You say you will come, and it takes you at your word, and the ruins fold up like a map being closed.
What you get is four minutes in a corridor outside a court that does not exist in this dimension, and a docket with your name on it that entitles you to be heard at a time of the court's choosing.
It is worth an enormous amount to certain people. It is also a debt.

b1.text:
Somebody has lived down there for a long time: a bed, a stove, four years of tins, and a wall covered in dates crossed off.
The last twenty are not crossed off. They are circled. And under the bed, in a bag packed and ready, is everything they meant to run with.

b2.text:
You walk beside a stranger to the edge of the ruins with an usher on the other side of them, and you talk to them the whole way about nothing at all, because that is what you can do.
At the boundary they thank you, and give you what is in their pocket, and go.
The usher, on the way past, looks at you for the first and only time, and does not write anything down, which one of you is quite sure is a kindness.

c1.text:
You write a name on a summons out of the Court of Eris, in pencil, because that is what is in your pocket.
It is accepted. That is the appalling part: it is accepted, and the usher turns ninety degrees onto a new bearing, and somewhere at the end of that bearing a person you have never met is going to look up.

c2.text:
You hand a dead functionary its paperwork back and it takes it and goes on.
On the fourth step it stops, comes back, and gives you something out of its coat: a token, brass, with a number on it. You have been given a place in a queue. Nobody who has ever seen one of these has been able to tell you whether that is good.

b1_m.text:
Somebody has lived down there for a long time: a bed, a stove, four years of tins, and a wall covered in dates.
The dates are in two columns. The left-hand column stops {four years ago|in the spring|abruptly}. The right-hand column does not, and the right-hand column is still being added to, and today's date is on it.

asides.cynical: {member}: "{Somebody wrote today's date on that wall.|Two columns. Two people.|They are still here.}"
asides.any: {member} {puts a hand on the stove, which is warm|reads the last four entries|counts the tins}

choices.text: Take what is worth taking and get out.
Work out what the two columns are counting.
Wait in the cellar for whoever is keeping the right-hand column.

b1_cols.text:
The left column is {days hidden|days down here|a tally of a hiding}. The right column is {days since|days owed|a countdown run the other way}, and it starts on the day the left one stops, which is the day the summons was issued.
Which means the person in this cellar is not hiding from the court. They are serving something, voluntarily, by a calendar, and it has {four years|a long time|eleven months} left to run.

b1_wait.text:
Four hours in somebody else's cellar with their stove and their tins and a wall of dates, which is a long four hours.
They come down the steps at {dusk|the usual time|about seven} with water and are not startled, and say, before anybody else can speak, that they have been expecting the court and that four people is more than the court usually sends.

c2_m.text:
You hand a dead functionary its paperwork back and it takes it and goes on, and on the fourth step it stops, and comes back, and holds the summons out again.
There is a second name on it now. It is not one of the party's names. It is a name one of the party {knows|recognises|has been avoiding}, and the ink is {wet|fresh|not dry}.

choices.text: Give it back again and walk away.
Ask it who wrote the second name.
Cross the second name out.

c2_who.text:
Nobody wrote it. That is the point of a summons out of that court: it {accrues|adds|fills in} as it goes, and the usher does not know the names on the paper it is carrying and has never been permitted to read one.
It says so plainly, in the manner of a clerk explaining a procedure, and then asks the party, for the first time in {four hundred years|a very long service|its entire career}, what the second name says.

c2_cross.text:
A pencil line through a name on a document out of the Court of Eris, drawn by somebody standing in a field of rubble who has decided that is a thing a person can do.
The name goes. So does the line. So, after about {four seconds|a moment|nine seconds}, does the pencil, out of the hand that was holding it, and the usher looks at the paper and then at the party with an expression that is very close to admiration.

e_graveyard_father.title: {The Relic In The Crypt|Grave Robbing For Fun & Profit|The Family Vault}

n0.emText:
Something fell in the night, took a corner off a tomb, and killed everything within four metres of where it stopped. Beyond four metres, nothing.
You know what this is before you get close. Everybody in the world knows, because they were told on the news: the Father is in orbit and He is coming down in pieces, and the pieces do this.
You are the reason He is up there.
n0.bubba: Bubba puts an arm across your chest without looking at you. "Sugar. Not this one. Aggia' ditto: not this one."

asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}
asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}
asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.fatalistic: {member} {sighs: "Well, we were going to die eventually."|shrugs: "If the reactor blows, at least it's quick."|mutters that the universe always finds a way to ruin your day|expects the worst and isn't disappointed}
